speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: PERMISSION TO EXPORT RAW SALMON-RETENTION IN CANADA OF RAW SOCKEYE, PINKS AND CHUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a matter of special importance to management and labour engaged in the salmon fishery industry in British Columbia.
As members will recall, the government late last fall withdrew its control on the export of certain species of raw salmon to the United States. This permitted United States buyers, who were offering higher prices, to obtain substantial quantities of Canadian raw salmon which otherwise would have been canned by our industry for domestic and export markets. Our canners, thus deprived of the raw materials, were obliged to suspend salmon canning operations in the latter part of the season.
The government has been concerned with the possibility of a more serious dislocation of salmon canning throughout the 1948 operating season. Separate submissions were heard from representatives of the canners, labour union and co-operatives, all of whom desired the maintenance of the British Columbia canning industry, notwithstanding some differences of opinion as to the sharing of their respective responsibilities in meeting this end. The government feels that some corrective steps must be taken to safeguard both fishermen and management. The most desirable solution seemed to be a measure of stabilization of the canning industry while at the same time assuring increased export of the raw material to the United States.
I wish, therefore, to announce that, effective immediately, British Columbia fishermen are permitted to export to the United States unrestricted quantities of raw spring salmon. Export of raw coho is also permitted, but only up to September 1 of this year.
Raw sockeye, pinks and chums, will be retained in Canada.
I want especially to emphasize that this decision is simply a ruling that is designed to give balanced treatment to management and 5849-1784
fishermen. It is not an embargo. It necessitates, of course, reasonable compromises on both sides.
I am satisfied that the decision reached by the cabinet will provide equitable safeguard for management in maintaining its canning industry and for fishermen by leaving the way open for them to take advantage of the higher prices paid on the United States market for springs and coho.
I might add here that the normal export to the United States of all species of canned, salted, smoked, cured frozen salmon is not, of course, affected by the ruling.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, April 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gregg for the second reading of Bill No. 196, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
When the house rose at eleven o'clock last evening I was pointing out the inadequacy of the amendments proposed in this legislation. Those inadequacies are in two or three different classes. In the first instance there is the inadequacy of the supplementary allowance that may be granted to a recipient of the war veterans allowance at the discretion of the board. The amount of the war veterans allowance is still 830 a month, but at the discretion of the board an additional supplementary allowance of $10 a month or $120 a year may be authorized.
In his remarks, which I have since had an opportunity of reading, the minister described the recipients of the allowance as consisting of three classes: first, the class who draw a pension as well as the war veterans allowance; second, the class composed of those who are non-pensioners but who draw the full amount of the allowance; and third, those recipients
who do not draw a pension nor the full allowance. The figures he gave as to the third class were something in the nature of 10,000.
My reading of the minister's remarks would indicate to me that he is to issue a directive to the department which will make mandatory the payment of the supplementary allowance to the first and second classes, but in respect of the third class he used the word "may" and I presume those recipients in the third class will submit their cases to the board for review. If the board decides they should receive the supplementary allowance, then at the discretion of the board an amount up to $120 a year may be granted. While the minister issues an order that the supplementary allowance will be paid to those in the first and second classes, no such mandatory instruction is contained in the bill. In the bill itself, the decision as to whether the amount of the supplementary allowance shall be granted is left to the discretion of the board. No doubt the veterans committee when the bill is referred to it will give consideration to the advisability of including in the bill specific instructions that the supplementary allowance be automatic to those who are pensioners drawing allowance or who are in receipt of full allowance, leaving only to the discretion of the board those who at the present time are not drawing the full allowance.
I consider the amendments inadequate in that they still maintain the means test. Although in certain respects, the permissible income has been changed, I am not at all clear from the minister's statement that there has been any increase in the permissible income. At page 2788 of Hansard he states:
In addition to the matter of increase, this bill rearranges what rvas known as "casual earnings" and raises the ceiling of permissible income under the act to $1,105 a year, or approximately $92: a month for married men and to $615 a year, or approximately $54 a month for single men.
Before this was introduced, the permissible income amounted to $615 for single men. It was made up of $365 as the maximum allowance, S125 for casual earnings, and $125 for other income, making the total of $615 as permissible income. I do not see, therefore, how there is any increase. There is a slight change in that there is the amalgamation of other income and casual earnings. In effect, a recipient of the war veterans allowance who does not go out and earn by his casual work $125 in a year, if he is in receipt of a pension in excess of $125 a year, may amalgamate those two and make up the total of $250. But at the same time the total permissible income of $615 is not exceeded. Encouragement is given to a man
War Veterans Allowance Act

not to work, and I suggest that is a wrong principle. It is better for the man himself and for the economy of the country to have a man in production and working, if he can find the opportunity to do so. Many of them make the opportunities in order to obtain casual work.
In addition-and this is the only increase I can see in the permissible income-there is the $120 which may be granted as a supplementary allowance at the discretion of the board or according to the instructions issued by the minister, as outlined by him last night. I do feel that if we are to encourage these middle-aged veterans to find work wherever they can, and improve their positions, rather than try to keep them down and make them live within the $615 or $735 a year-a pretty slim sum in these days-we should raise that ceiling much higher than it is now. I believe it was the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) who said it should be raised to the minimum income exemptions. We should encourage these men to work for the good of the country and of themselves rather than to rely entirely upon their pensions or their allowances.
One other inadequacy I did not have the opportunity to mention last night, is that of the amendments in respect to extending the allowances to other groups of veterans. At various other times, during this session and in others, I have mentioned the need for providing allowances to other groups of veterans. In the present debate other members have mentioned exactly the same thing, and have drawn attention to some groups about which I intend to speak again this afternoon. I refer to them because I believe it is only by continually impressing upon the government the need these men have, and the demand there is among veterans of all classes in every section of the country that their comrades be included in these allowances and be provided with a decent standard of living, that we can hope to get some consideration, should the committee be prepared to make recommendations along these lines.
The first class I wish to mention is that of the soldiers who went from Canada during the first world war and who, through no fault of their own, did not get closer to a theatre of war than Great Britain. This group may be divided into two classes. There were those who, through ill health incurred in Great Britain, were debarred from going overseas to France. I am certain all hon. members will have vivid recollections of or will have read about the hardships the first Canadian expeditionary force suffered while in training at Salisbury Plains during the winter of 1914-15.

Their living conditions were bad. There were no huts built, as there were in the latter days of the last war. They had to live in tents during an extremely bad winter, where the mud, rain and general conditions were appalling. That is a well established fact.
Many of those men suffered from meningitis and other diseases which in some instances impaired their health for the rest of their lives, and in any event denied them the opportunity of taking their places with their comrades in France.
Then there was another class of men, those who, on account of special training in the nonpermanent militia of pre-war days or because of their civilian training, were retained in Great Britain for special purposes, to instruct other men who went overseas. But, through no fault of their own, and against their desire, those men were kept in England. The records show that many individuals applied time and again to their commanding officers to be allowed to go overseas, but in the interest of the service they were retained.
No one is going to suggest that conditions in Great Britain were as hazardous during the first world war as during the second. We do know, however, that bombs were dropped by enemy aircraft. The Canadian camp at Shorn-eliffe was bombarded. Zeppelins came over; and I remember vividly seeing a map published by the Daily Mail which showed where the bombs had been dropped during the first world war. A number of bombs were dropped with surprising accuracy along the Brixton road leading out of London and there w'ere many casualties. Veterans of the second world war who remained in Great Britain are regarded as having served in a theatre of war, while veterans of the first world war who were denied the privilege of taking their places with their comrades in France, who were retained in Great Britain against their will, are denied this privilege. I do not know the exact number of these men, but it is not great, and I submit that these allowances should be extended to them.
I come now to the question of our comrades who served with the forces of His Majesty other than the Canadian forces, usually referred to as imperials. Every branch of the legion and other veteran organizations across Canada have been recommending for years that these men should receive more generous treatment at the hands of Canada than they have received in the past. I have here a resolution passed by the imperial veterans of Canada in Winnipeg. It first points out that the imperials living in Canada have contributed in great measure to the progress of Canada. It then goes on to explain the contri-

War Veterans Allowance Act
bution they have made' to Canada, both in peace and in war, and finally it says:
And whereas there are imperial veterans long resident in this country, who are now Canadian citizens, living under the most intolerable conditions, with a lower standing of living than those on relief.
It may be said that that is probably an exaggeration. I have here a copy of the British Legion Pension Guide, and on pages 8 and 9 there appears the scale of pensions paid to ex-imperials. Men and boys of the Royal Navy, marines, privates, gunners, leading aircraftmen and aircraftmen of the R.A.F. who are 100 per cent pensionable receive forty-five shillings a week, which translated into terms of Canadian currency equals $36 per month. I am not suggesting that there are many imperial veterans living in Canada who are receiving 100 per cent pension, and they would hardly be affected by the war veterans allowances. I merely cite that as an example.
When you come down to the lower brackets you find that an imperial receiving a 20 per cent pension gets exactly nine shillings per week paj'able every four weeks, which amounts to approximately $8 per month. I am not surprised that the imperial veterans in Winnipeg passed a resolution stating that men who are trying to get along on $8 per month are living in squalor and under a low standard of living. I feel at this time that we should recognize the fact that we have admitted these imperial veterans into the fellowship of Canadian citizenship; they are now Canadian citizens, and many of them have long residence in Canada.
There are two classes of imperial veterans. I would call the attention of the minister and the committee to the fact that many of these imperials were resident in Canada prior to their enlistment in the British services. According to the regulations, if they were resident in Canada immediately prior to enlistment they would be eligible for an allowance. But if they had left Canada three months, six months, a year or any period of time longer than that before enlisting, they were not eligible.
Many British reservists who were living in Canada in 1914 rejoined their old regiments. They are entitled to an allowance, while Canadian born men who had resided in Canada for many years, but who for one reason or another found themselves in Great Britain when war broke out, are barred from these allowances because they were not domiciled in Canada at the time of enlistment. Some of these men were students who were completing their education in Great Britain in 1914, and they are barred.
Then there is the larger group made up of those who migrated to Canada after the war finished in 1918. They were encouraged to come here, and many of them have lived here ever since. They have contributed much to the development of this country. In many cases their sons and daughters fought in the ranks of the Canadian forces during the second world war, and many of these men joined up locally with the veterans guard or other organizations. The time has come when we should not have any hyphenated Canadians. The imperial soldier who has taken out Canadian citizenship should be considered a Canadian and should have all the rights of Canadian citizenship. He has in other respects.
Finally there are the other groups which I shall not take the time to enumerate, because I have mentioned them on previous occasions. I intend to bring up their cases in the committee. I repeat that I feel that this bill provides inadequate amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. In the first place, the supplementary allowances will in many cases be inadequate to meet the needs of the recipient. Second, the ceiling of permissible income has not been raised high enough to encourage men to work and thereby raise their standard of living. Finally, it is inadequate because it makes no provision for these other groups of pensioners who are in urgent need of allowances.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I must say that this bill is one of the most disappointing I have seen brought down in this house. I am fully satisfied that the members of the veterans affairs committee, all of whom are. veterans, feel the same way about it, and that they will do their best in the committee to secure the improvements that are being asked for in this debate on second reading. My reason for rising to take part in the debate is the hope that those of us who speak as nonveterans will be able to reinforce the views of the. veterans themselves who are members of the committee and help them to secure a much better War Veterans Allowance Act than is yet in prospect.
I am sure that last evening we were all delighted with what the minister was able to say, supported by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and others, concerning the way in which the old soldiers themselves have expressed no jealousy about the improvements made in benefits for veterans of world war II and have put on no pressure campaigns on their own behalf. I also want to say that
War Veterans Allowance Act

we in this house who are non-veterans are thrilled at the way in which the veteran members of the house really go to bat on behalf of their comrades of both wars, and we are pleased too that this is no partisan matter. But I believe it should be said, as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Gibson) pointed out in another debate, that the desire for the best possible deal for Canada's veterans is shared not only by the veterans themselves on behalf of their comrades, but also by the civilian population of the country generally. All of us want the best possible deal for our veterans, and I hope that the debate now taking place and the speeches now being made on all sides of the house will reinforce the members of the committee as they make their recommendations and seek to improve the bill.
I said at the outset that the legislation struck me as one of the bitterest disappointments I have seen brought down in this house in the form of legislation. In fact I felt that to a certain extent both the house and the country generally have been misled. On the 19th of December the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced the proposed increases both in the disability pension and in the war veterans allowance. His reference to the war veterans allowance was very brief. This was it:
The amendment will authorize the war veterans allowance board to grant supplementary allowances up to $10 a month in cases of need for veterans and widows who, through age and infirmity, are unable to provide for their own maintenance. The board will be authorized to make the supplementary allowances retroactive to October 1, or to any subsequent date, as the circumstances of individual eases may require.
When we heard that announcement, while we recognized that there was in it a means test qualification, still, brief as the announcement was, it. pointed to an increase of $10 a month, and I think it is correct to say that we in this house and veterans and veterans organizations generally thought that that was a flat ten-dollar increase to those veterans who are on the war veterans allowance. A few weeks later, to be exact on February 16, after there had been considerable expression of displeasure with the announcements of December 19 having to do both with the disability pension and with the war veterans allowance, the Prime Minister made another announcement indicating that certain further increases were being proposed in the disability pension. On that occasion the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), who has just spoken, asked the Prime Minister, as reported at page 1288 of Hansard, this question:
Is provision being made for increases under the War Veterans Allowance Act?

Although the member addressed his question to the Prime Minister, the answer was made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) in these words:
The amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act are still under study, and the proposals will be completed before the end of the present week.
For my part I took it from that statement that, just as there had been some improvement, slight as it was, in the proposals respecting the pension act between December 19 and February 16, so we might anticipate some improvement in the proposed amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. But it appears now that the bill before us simply implements the announcement of December 19. I can see in it nothing beyond what we were offered at that time.
A little later the resolution preceding this bill was put on the order paper. Reading it we were still uncertain just what wras in store, but there were at least two phrases in it that gave us hope. It said that there would be increased permissible income, and supplementary allowances. Those were the two things in which we rvere mainly interested -an increase in the allowance itself to the burnt-out veteran or to his wddow, and an increase in the over-all ceiling on income allowed to these people. When that resolution was being considered in the committee of the whole the Minister of Veterans Affairs made a brief statement upon it. He said at page 2716 of Hansard:
In the main it is the purpose of the bill to improve the amounts payable to the beneficiaries under that legislation.
Later in the same short statement he said:
In the main this bill is designed to increase the amounts payable to them, and to deal with other subsidiary matters indicated in the resolution.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that during all the stages that led up to the introduction of this bill we were led to believe we were to get in the main precisely those two things: a worthwhile increase in the amount of the war veterans allowance, and an increase in the total permissible income allowed to those in receipt of this benefit. I submit, sir, that with respect to many thousands of those on the war veterans allowance we get neither-neither an increase in the amount of the allowance the veteran will receive, nor an increase in the total income permitted to allowance recipients.
I was surprised, but in one sense pleased, to learn from the minister's remarks yesterday that there are about 16,000 recipients of the war veterans allowance who will be entitled automatically to receive the $10 a mouth

War Veterans Allowance Act
increase. I say I was surprised and in only one sense pleased to learn there were that many who would benefit in this way, but on the other hand I was saddened to realize that there are that many veterans, mostly of world war I, whose circumstances are such, who are living so far below the ceiling, that they will immediately qualify for that S10. It does seem to me that that simply is not good enough.
I was glad that the previous speaker, the hon. member for Nanaimo, pointed gut in detail that the minister is not really justified in talking about new ceilings and about increased permissible income. It is true that by the terms of the bill before us there is to be what looks like an increase in the amount of income from any source which a veteran may earn apart from his allowance, but that is offset by removing from the existing statute the clause that permitted S125 of casual income. To be fair, we must say that from this side of the house we have asked that the distinction between these two kinds of income be abolished, because of the fact that it has forced veterans to move from one job to another. But when we asked that that distinction be abolished, we hoped there would be a real increase in permissible income and not just the bracketing of the two figures already there.
As the previous speaker pointed out, under the act as it now stands, without the amendments proposed by this bill, a single veteran has the right to earn, in addition to the $365 allowance, $125 from any source and $125 casual income, which is a total of $615 a year. If this bill is enacted in its present form, the ceiling for the single veteran will still be that same figure, $615 a year. There is one slight qualification we should always make, and that is that $25 a year from unearned income is granted; but it hardly alters the case at all. In the case of the single veteran the ceiling is $615 a year, and the ceiling as a result of the proposals made by the minister will still be $615.
Similarly, with the married veteran, the present situation is that he can draw an allowance of $730 a year and make $250 from any source and $125 casual income, a total of $1,105. All that this bill does is to bracket the $250 and the $125 into one sum of $375, which means that after the bill is passed he *will be allowed to make $375 from any source, on top of the $730 allowance, which means that the ceiling is the same, $1,105.
May I point out that I have been speaking thus far, in connection with this phase of the matter, about the ceiling. There is another
way in which to describe this, namely, to use the language of the act. The act does not talk about a ceiling, as the Old Age Pensions Act does. It talks about other incomes which the veteran is entitled to earn, and if this amendment goes through, the veteran will be entitled to earn other incomes, if he is single, of $250 a year and, if he is married, $375 a year.
I ask the house to face this shameful fact, that these are precisely the figures written into the War Veterans Allowance Act in 1930. The other income allowed to the veteran has not been changed at all by any amendments made to the act since it was first passed in 1930.
I feel that the committee should know the temper of the house, of the non-veteran members and of the country about this matter, and they should make full use of the right they have in the veterans committee, which we do not have in committee of the whole, to make recommendations calling for increases involving the expenditure of money. I say they should make use of that right to obtain a substantial increase in this ceiling on the amount of income allowed to the burnt-out pensioner.
I think the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was most reasonable in suggesting the income tax exemption figure of $750 single and $1,500 married. Incidentally, speaking of the life * history of the War Veterans Allowance Act, I was interested in making this discovery. The act was first passed in 1930, and amended in 1936, 1938, 1946, and now in 1948, and on every occasion but one there has been an increase in the salaries of some members of the board. On that one occasion when there was not an increase in salaries there was an increase in the number of members. In other words it has always been possible to find more money for the members of the board. I do not begrudge it, but having regard to the fact that the other income allowed burnt-out pensioners has not been increased at all from what it was when the act was passed in 1930, and also that prior to this supplementary allowance, about which I shall have something to say in a moment, there has been only one increase in the amount of the allowance, and it will be seen that the benefit to the veteran is really not very a good record for this parliament.
Let me put it this way. I do not want to be partisan and to put all the blame in this instance on the government. There is a tradition that veterans legislation is parliament's legislation, and that is borne out by the way in which these matters are referred to the veterans committee. If I speak strongly about the matter it is in the hope that it will reinforce the members of the veterans
War Veterans Allowance Act

committee to be-as the minister said last night, though I am afraid he misused the word-generous to the veterans. This legislation, certainly with respect to the ceilings, is not generous at all.
I should like to say a further word about the ceiling question. If the bill goes through in the form in which it stands, the minister and his department might as well know that there will be considerable protest against it during the next few months, and that they will run into administrative difficulties. I would be prepared to predict that a year from now they will come back and ask us to raise the ceiling on the income.
If I may quote a parallel case, I would point out that in 1943, when by order in council the first increase was made in the old age pension in the amount of $5 a month, the government did not see fit to increase the ceiling of pensioners' income. In only a matter of a few months the then minister of finance, now Minister of Justice, was faced with the fact not only that it was not good enough but that there were administrative difficulties, and the government raised the ceiling at least by the amount of the increase that had been made in the pension itself.
And so I say. with respect to this measure, that even though it does include only a 810 supplementary allowance, there should have been at least that much increase in the overall ceiling. In other words, the ceiling should now be not less than $735 a year for single veterans and $1,225 for married. These are not the figures I would suggest. I would suggest $750 and $1,500. But if the minister would at least go that far, his figures would provide an increase in the ceiling to take care of the supplementary allowance itself, and permit all burnt-out pensioners and their widows to receive it.
With regard to the supplementary allowance, there too I want to keep my language moderate, but it does seem to me that we have been misled. I listened closely to the member for Nanaimo, and I thought he was under the impression that some veterans might get that $120 a year on top of the $615 ceiling to which they are held. If the hon. member will look into the bill, which I cannot refer to by section while we are on second reading, he will discover that the supplementary allowance is payable to the veteran only within the $615 or $1,105 ceiling. In other words, if a veteran is now drawing his $365 a year or $30.41 a month-a single veteran-and he is now making a total other income of S20.84 a month, that brings him to $615 and he will not be able to get the $10 supplementary

allowance. Neither will it be available to the married veteran now getting $730 a year or $60.83 a month, if he is already making the limit of $375 a year or $31.25 a month, for he will already be at the ceiling of $1,105.
The veteran will get the $10 supplementary allowance only if he is unemployable to such an extent, and lacking in economic resources to such an extent, that he is practically living on nothing more than the burnt-out pension itself.
It seems to me that the least this parliament would like to do, when we talk about the $10 supplementary allowance, is to do it right across the board the way it is done when freight rates are increased: ten dollars a month to every veteran on the bumt-out pension, whatever his situation may be. If that had been the proposal of the minister, some of us would not have smiled as we did the other night when he used the word "generous".
I strongly urge, Mr. Speaker, that the committee battle it out with the minister and send him back to the cabinet with the insistence that that $10 increase be right across the board; that the increase in the ceiling be not the misleading one we have in this bill but an actual effective increase which will make it possible for all veterans on the allowance to get this extra $10.
I should like to say a few words with reference specifically to the case of non-pensioned veterans' widows who are covered by this legislation. It is not many years since there was no provision for women whose husbands, when they died, were on less than 50 per cent pension. I am glad to see that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) has just come in, because he is one who, in years not long since, fought hard, along with others of us in this house, to get the government to make an allowance for these women. A measure to make such provision was first brought in in 1943. For a few years-in fact down until 1946 -it was a matter of an annual vote, but in 1946 provision for an allowance to these widows of non-pensioned veterans was written into the act which we are now amending. Making it statutory was a step in the right direction. The situation now is that when anything is done for the burnt-out pensioners, it is done automatically at the same time for the widows covered under this act. But on their behalf I want to say that the proposed increase of $10 a month should go to all of them without any question. Because of the way in which the proposed act is worded, they will be subject to the means test and they will get that extra $10 a month or $120 a year only if they are

War Veterans Allowance Act
under the ceiling of $615 a year which applies in the case of a widow without a child or children.
I put in a special word for these women, because their situation is a difficult one. Many of them have had the experience of seeing their husbands who were on no pension at all or on a 40 per cent disability pension, suffer a good deal in the later years of their lives from their war experiences. When those husbands pass on, the widows are in just as difficult circumstances as are the widows of other veterans. Yet they must take this legislation which is not something they receive as of right; and the very fact that that is so makes it necessary that the provision for them be much more generous than it has been.
When we talk about the widows, the same considerations come into play that have already been discussed by others who have spoken in this debate. I refer, for example, to the question of service in England during the last war. My attention has been brought to the position of many widows in my own city and in other cities, women whose husbands served only in England during the last war and therefore could not qualify even for this allowance.
I was present last year, Mr. Speaker, when a group of these women-other members might have been present too, but I am not sure about that-had a conference here in Ottawa with the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who at that time was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs; I understand he has recently resigned that position. On the occasion of that meeting in the Liberal caucus room on the fourth floor these women, speaking on behalf of the organization of non-pensioned widows, presented their requests one by one. With regard to a number of their requests the hon. member for Rosthern could make no commitment; but when they asked for the inclusion of England as a theatre of war in world war I, the hon. member for Rosthern, in so far as he could as a member outside of the cabinet, made a commitment to these women. He said: "I can give you the assurance that next year, although you will not get some of the things you want, but you will get an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act that will make service in England in the last war count for the purpose of this act."
I know that the women of that organization have counted during the year on that one specific improvement being made. I realize that the hon. member for Rosthern was not in a position to commit the cabinet. I also realize that he has made about the country a number of statements of the kind which do not seem
to get government backing. But these women took it as a solemn undertaking from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. As a matter of fact they saw the previous minister as well, but I was not with them on that occasion. There is keen disappointment on their part that the change is not being made. I strongly urge upon the members of the committee, representing, as they do, the House of Commons to deal with this phase of the matter as parliament and as the country would wish them to do. The same considerations apply to the imperial veterans now living in Canada, but since this matter has been well developed by others, I need not go into it in any further detail.
Another thing I should like to say on behalf of the non-pensioned veterans' widows who are covered by this legislation is that I hope consideration will be given to their request to be included in' the matter of hospitalization. On one occasion when I raised this question the former Minister of Veterans Affairs seemed to misunderstand it and to think that they were asking, or that I was asking on their behalf, that room be found for them in veterans' hospitals. That is not their request at all. They are asking rather that financial provision be made for them when they themselves require hospitalization. So long as the amounts are as they are, I feel that that is a request which the government ought to meet.
Someone has said that this whole War Veterans Allowance Act is in the nature of social security legislation for the veterans. I think that is a good way to describe it. If it is to be social security legislation, let it have in it some element of real security; let it not be just a matter of charity as it is at the present time.
So, Mr. Speaker, I leave it at that. I feel that the amount of this allowance should be $50 a month for a single person and $100 a month for a married person; that the ceiling: should be effectively raised and not just in the manner in which this bill does it; that service in England in the last war should count; that imperial veterans now in Canada should be considered; and, as I have already said, that the widows covered under this act should be given by the government the benefit of hospitalization.
I conclude by once again expressing my earnest hope that the committee, when it deals with this matter, will not only deal with it as veterans, which they are, and not only on the non-partisan basis on which they have approached these matters from session to session and parliament to parliament, but that they will realize that the non-veteran mem-
War Veterans Allowance Act

bers of this house and the civilian population of Canada generally want a much better deal for our veterans than is provided in the bill now before us.
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview); The motion before you, Mr. Speaker, is for the second reading of the War Veterans Allowance Act, and I wish to draw the attention of the minister to one particular class of people who come under it. The original act was passed in 1930 to give some reasonable allowance to *those who fought in the South African war and world war I; and recently those veterans who served in the northwest rebellion, the forgotten men as far as veterans affairs go, were also included. Many of these men are located in the maritimes; a number of them are in the, Toronto district; some are in Saskatchewan and some in Winnipeg. They have received practically nothing. They were given grants of land, 160 acres each principally in Saskatchewan and northern Ontario, but they were given no travelling allowance to get to their land, with the result that many men never even saw it.
These were the men who started the militia eight years after the Mackenzie government passed the first militia act. They left their vocations and received no pay for serving, except fifty cents a month. Most of them paraded twice a week and on Sundays; they went to camp; and the fifty cents they received was put back into the company fund in order to build up the militia. Then came the South African war, and later the two great wars. Some of these men are in desperate circumstances today. I believe it was only in 1944 that they first received assistance under this legislation, but then those in charge of the act brought into effect what they call the means test. That was the meanest thing we have ever done in this house, because at the present time these men cannot even rent a small room with the amount they are receiving. Many small estates have been required to pay back the amount received in old age pensions and all that sort of thing. I remember one man who was with Sir John A. Macdonald when he lied; I shall not give his name, because I do not think it is necessary. He was in the press gallery here, and he wrote many articles on this subject in the Globe and also in the Mail.
I believe these men have been very poorly treated. They marched across lake Superior in the depth of winter when the temperature was 46 degrees below zero. They lived on dog biscuits and hardtack, and saved that country from being ravaged; and probably

they opened the eyes of the whole civilized world to the possibilities of the great prairie provinces which today are doing so much for this country. The other day I received a letter from my kind and good friend the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker), who is always engaged in good works, not only within his own party but in association with others in this house. The letter was from a member of the northwest field force in British Columbia who with others presented a brief to the veterans affairs committee two years ago. I believe he wanted to obtain $160 cash in lifeu of the 160 acres of land he had been granted. Nothing has been done about it since the committee got the brief.
The way in which these men have been used is the meanest thing I have ever heard of. The other day I was told of a man who had been one of these veterans, and whose son in later years became associated with the university of Toronto in connection with the training of football and hockey teams. He died, and when they came to settle up his estate it was found to be worth $837. Then along came the government to apply the means test, and asked that $600 be paid back. I must say of the former minister of veterans affairs that I always found him willing to assist the veterans; his heart was in the work. The present minister was for some time associated with the great university of New Brunswick, and holds the highest military decoration in the world. I do hope he will look into the cases of these members of the northwest field force, because they certainly have been given shabby treatment, though they were the backbone and founders of the militia of this country. From 1885 on through the South African war and the two world wars they, their children and their children's children have been serving in the forces.
I do not wish to detain the house longer. I have dealt already with the other matters involved in this bill and the other measures relating to the veterans. 1 or that reason I am prepared to give way now to the soldiers in other parts of the house.

If we had [DOT] allowed our production to increase, as it could have done with the return of three-quarters of a million of our finest producers from overseas, then we should have enough surplus production to enable each of our people to have a thousand dollars' worth, and still take care of the exports necessary in relation to our external obligations.
Let us keep in mind what I have said as we consider the bill before us, which will render available to the recipient of a war veterans allowance, if he is married, the sum of $1,170 a year.
It may be argued that the country cannot afford financially to give a larger allowance. A sound financial system would overcome that difficulty. What cannot be defended to the satisfaction of any logical mind, is the niggardliness of the means test which is applied not only in this act but in the Old Age Pensions Act and in other acts.
Surely a man should be free to earn what he needs and what he can earn, without risking the loss of his allowance! Let the government and the house once more lay down the principle commonly accepted during the war that no man or woman should be worse off because of going into the services, and no one who stayed out of the services ought to be better off because of having stayed out. The principle ought also to apply to servicemen's wives.
The Canadian parliament is in duty and honour bound, first, to make of Canada a home fitting for heroes; second, to make it possible for every Canadian hero to find in Canada a fitting home, and, third, to render it possible and encouraging for every Canadian hero to raise up a family of hero sons to strengthen and bless our country in the days to come.
May I urge upon the minister and members of the committee that if the Canadian parliament is to discharge these duties they must bring back a bill far more generously and courageously drafted than is the hidebound effort that parliament is now considering and is about to submit to the committee for what I hope will be drastic revision.
May I urge upon the minister and members of the committee that parliament expects the minister and the committeemen to do their duty, not as the treasury board sees that duty but as the progressive, pulsating Canadian people see it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like 'to add a word or two to what has already been said with reference to Bill No. 196 to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act.
The house has listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) and other members who have expressed their views. What concerns me most at the moment is not what has already been said but what has not been said and might be said regarding the war veterans allowances.
In his opening remarks the minister stated that the benefits relating to this bill would apply in the main to a small proportion of the old soldiers of the first great war. He made mention that only 25,000 out of approximately 200,000 soldiers are receiving aid from their country. The complete summary, as tabulated,
is as follows:
Veterans, all wars	 26,106
Widows, all wars	 4,790
Orphans, all wars	 53
Total	 30,949
First, may I say that I hope the present minister and those who are closely associated with him, the pension board and all who are called upon to make decisions, will never permit the injustice to be done to the veterans of world war II that was done to many of those gallant veterans of world war I. No onus or responsibility can be placed upon the present minister, but it can be placed upon the department which had to do with the policy that resulted in a reduction of many pensions. There is not in this house a veteran of world war I who cannot recall an instance in his own riding of some veteran who enjoyed a 100 per cent pension who was dumbfounded to open his mail and find a letter from the Department of Veterans Affairs advising him that his case had been re-examined and that there would be a reduction in his pension.
To emphasize my point, I should like to draw attention to a case I have in mind of a late pensioner whose family lives in Kingston. This man had had a 100 per cent pension for fourteen years when he was notified by the pension board that his pension would be reduced to 45 per cent. Those familiar with the Pension Act will readily understand the reduction to 45 per cent. It meant that his widow and family would be deprived of any pension at his death, the act requiring that 55 per cent pension is necessary at the time of death for a family to qualify for pension.
This man was seriously ill and receiving treatment in Christie Street hospital. His wife, then in her early sixties, was doing the best

War Veterans Allowance Act
she could to get along. What happened? The veteran, was heart-broken, and died shortly afterwards. I might add that I came to Ottawa to see the pension board on behalf of this widow. I received a courteous hearing and had every reason to expect that the case would be considered. However, for reasons best known to the pension board at the time, that was the end of it.
There seemed to be a feeling at that time that there were too many receiving 100 per cent pension. A special board was arranged to probe into the case but the old soldier had very little recourse. I trust and hope that those veterans of world war II who are receiving pensions will not be dealt with as ruthlessly as have many of the veterans of world war I.
I might also cite another case, that of a pensioner who received notice that his pension had been reduced from 100 per cent to 5 per cent. This man had a family of seven children and it took him nearly twelve months to have h'is pension returned. The purpose of amending this act is to make provision for the neglected child of a veteran.
The pension board should not take too much credit for caring for certain types of veterans who happen to lose an eye, a limb or an arm. The act is specific as to what should be done in such cases. But there are the borderline cases dealing with nervous disorders, heart or cancer. In so many cases the benefit of the doubt seems to go against the soldier instead of in his favour, and such should not .be the case. I emphasize as strongly as I can that I think the benefit of the doubt should be given to the soldier.
I should like to cite a case of a veteran of world war II and I do this because I feel that many similar cases should receive further attention. This man's name is Herbert J. Leach. His number is C-1072 and he enlisted in the R.C.H.A. at Kingston. On January 3 he was killed in action, leaving a widow and two children, a boy and a girl. This man enlisted in 1939 and those who are familiar with the circumstances will realize that his number of C-1072 is not a boxcar number.
The daughter has since married. When this soldier proceeded overseas his boy was just ten years of age. Upon the soldier's death his widow received $60 a month plus $15 a month for the boy until he was sixteen years of age. Unfortunately the boy happens to be below normal and his mother is left with the responsibility of caring for him. She has been refused any further veterans allowance by the!pension board. This particular case was brought to my attention and I in turn brought it to the attention of the minister and the department.
The application was substantiated by a certificate from the family doctor which stated:
This is to certify that Victor Leach, aged nineteen, of 51 Raglan road, Kingston, Ontario, is totally and completely incapacitated on account of meningitis at two years and is an epileptic and mentally defective.
R. R. MacGregor, M.D.
In order to support her child, the mother was forced to take a position as laundress for which she receives $18 a week. Her own allowance as a widow was 860, which has recently been increased to $70. The pension board decided that no pension should be paid to the child, stating that no pension shall be paid to a child who, if a boy, is over the age of sixteen years, except when such child and those responsible for his maintenance are without adequate resources.
I think the house will agree that it is a shame and disgrace when the widow of a man who has given his life for his country, a man who paid the supreme sacrifice and left a child unable to care for himself, is turned down by the department. I might add also that the mother of this boy is faced with an extra expense. The boy recently had scarlet fever which necessitated his being in hospital for twenty-one days, the bill incurred for this illness amounting to $111. I want to emphasize what I mentioned a moment ago, that we do not want the veterans of world war II to be treated as the veterans of world war I have been. I am not blaming the minister because these cases came up before he took over the portfolio. I submit that in every case the benefit of the doubt should go to the dependent or the returned soldier rather than to the department or the government.
I should like to draw attention to another case of hardship being visited upon a veteran student. Only last week there was brought to my attention the case of a veteran student who is ill in the Kingston General hospital and receiving treatment. This boy is married and, like many others, carries protection under a hospital insurance plan. On arrival in hospital he was presented with form 706 compiled by the Department of Veterans Affairs, a copy of which I hold in my hand. This form necessitates his turning over to the Department of Veterans Affairs any hospital benefits which he would receive under the insurance plan. This boy is being penalized for trying to look after his wife and family. Any other veteran who happened to enter the hospital and who was not under the plan would have his total hospital expenses taken care of by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
To explain this case further, I might mention that the veteran benefits to this boy will expire
War Veterans Allowance Act

in October of this year. What concerns this veteran and his wife is that the hospital benefits to which he has personally contributed were taken away from him by the Department of Veterans Affairs. This means that on and after October 1 this veteran and his family will not be entitled to any hospitalization.
I do not know whether the minister is familiar with this form and I can send him one if he wishes. Great hardship is being suffered by these veterans. It is a mimeographed form. This sort of treatment is something that should not happen.
I shall say nothing further. I have mentioned these two cases and I would refer again in conclusion to that boy. I know that under sections 20 and 21 of the Pension Act the minister has power to look into these cases if he sees fit to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to be permitted to make a few observations on Bill No. 196, which has to do with the amending of certain clauses of the War Veterans Allowance Act. It is not my purpose to speak at any length because I am a member of the veterans affairs committee to which we have been informed this bill is to be submitted, and where I am confident its merits and deficiencies will be thoroughly reviewed.
The War Veterans Allowance Act was originally set up to provide for needy veterans who would normally not be in receipt of disability pension. Perhaps I may be permitted to enumerate its main features. The veteran must be sixty years of age, permanently unemployable or, having served in a theatre of actual warfare, incapable of maintaining himself because of economic handicaps combined with physical or mental disability or insufficiency.
The maximum allowance paid under this act for a single veteran was $30.41 a month, and the married veteran received double that or S60.83 a month. Casual and other earnings were not to exceed a total of $250. The maximum allowance for a widow was only $365 a year, or one dollar a day, unless there were children, in which case the allowance was increased to $730 a year, or $60.83 a month.
The bill before the house is to make certain amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act of 1946, all of which I do not care to discuss in detail at this time but I do wish to refer to one which I think should be commented upon. Other amendments could have been proposed which would have received the commendation of the whole house. I am not so sure that all these amendments do.

For instance, the amendment to increase the over-all income earned to $250 a year I cannot see is of very great advantage to the veteran. There are several minor amendments but I shall refer only to the provision for a supplementary allowance. It must be noted that the bill does make provision for the payment of a supplementary allowance of $120 if increase is approved by the board. We are assuming, of course, that the board will in most cases make provision for the payment of this supplementary allowance. But if this supplementary allowance is paid the bill states that the amount must not exceed the difference between the actual income of the recipient and the permissible income applicable in his case. In essence this simply means, if I interpret the bill correctly, that the veteran who receives the supplementary allowance of $10 a month will have his permissible income reduced accordingly, so that he will be, in actual fact, no better off than he was before.
It seems to me that about all that this bill does is to grant the old veteran the right to work harder in order to supplement his income without being deprived of his allowance. Under present conditions of high living costs it is apparent to all that he will certainly have to find some source from which to augment his income or else go hungry. So the government introduces this legislation in order that those able to work may make a few extra dollars to eke out an existence. But many are unable to work; some are completely unemployable because of age or disability. These men will now receive the ridiculously low sum of $40.41 a month allowance.
I do not think these war veterans will be very happy about legislation that makes no greater provision for them than this. They do not complain. They accepted their lot in the first world war and they are accepting it now. But there are many of us in this house who do not consider this legislation as fair to these fine citizens of Canada as it should be. I feel that all veterans throughout this land will be disappointed with this bill. It provides only a pittance where plenty could be provided. Canada has the money; the government has the money. We need only cite the $700 million surplus which it is estimated the government will have on this year's operations to prove that point. _
These veterans served Canada well in her hour of need. The minister stated last evening that they rendered honourable fighting service to this country. We all agree with that remark, but actions speak louder than words. If they rendered that valuable service, then

War Veterans Allowance Act
all I can say of this bill is that it is cheap and not worthy of a grateful country. Canada should pay for value received. These men are burnt-out in their fifties and sixties because of their participation in early life in the first world war. They may have no visible war scars, no very great war disability, but they are nevertheless some of the most pathetic casualties of the first world struggle.
I wish to associate myself with what has been said by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and to urge upon the government that they increase the allowance to at least $50 a month for single man, $100 a month for married men, and to widows in receipt of the allowance to $50 a month. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that these amounts are little enough; indeed, they are much too small because I am sure that few people today can keep a household together on $50 a month. If these veterans deserve an allowance at all, and I do not believe any member of this house would suggest that they are not deserving, then the allowance ought at least to be large enough to permit these old veterans or their widows to live in decency and reasonable comfort in their declining years. They should not always have to live in the shadow of poverty in a country which is rated as one of the wealthiest nations in the world.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not my intention to hold the measure up, but I have a few words to say before it goes to the committee.
I am not going to argue the merits or the demerits of the bill. I will leave that for the veterans affairs committee, because I do not think that what we say in .the house will have very much influence on that committee. At least that has been my experience in serving on similar committees in the past. There are, however, one or two points which are not covered by the bill and which I should now like to emphasize.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) went thoroughly into the financial aspects of the matter and there is no necessity for me to repeat what he has said. I notice that the bill makes no provision to care for incapacitated veterans who may be residing in the United States. I have had several cases myself which I have taken up with the war veterans allowance board. These war veterans of the first world war came back to Canada in 1919, some of them with war disabilities, and if they had remained in the country and fought their pension claims they could have established their right to pension.
Older veterans in the house will remember that in the years from 1919 to 1925 there was not much opportunity for employment in Canada, with the result that hundreds of veterans who served in an actual theatre of war could not secure employment here and had to go to the United States. Many of these veterans are in the United States today; and representations have been made to me, as no doubt they have been made to the minister himself, asking that something be done for veterans residing in the United States, having dependents and being totally incapacitated and hospitalized. These men have hospital bills, maintenance and so forth and are being taken care of by the United States government, and representations have been made to me to find out whether under the regulations it would be possible to extend the war veterans allowance privileges to veterans in that category while they are residing across the line.
Under the act as it has existed until now the stand taken by the department, and rightly so, in accordance with the regulations, was that this measure was not construed as a war veterans pension measure but as a social measure, more or less an old age pension arrangement for the incapacitated veteran, and that as such it could not be applied outside the country. However, if a man and his family returned to Canada, after a certain length of time in this country he could establish a claim.
I would point out, however, that in many of these cases the man is hospitalized and lacks the necessary means to come back to the country, and therefore he is a recipient of charity in the United States, despite the fact, mind you, that his present condition is attributable to services rendered in a theatre of war for this country, Canada.
I know from past experience with the minister in respect of veterans problems that he is sympathetic, that he understands those problems, and I suggest to him now and to the members of the veterans affairs committee that serious consideration be given to the question of amending this act so that veterans in the United States, in the position I have indicated, may receive the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
The war veterans pension is paid outside Canada. A man may reside in any part of the world and his pension will follow him. I see no reason why this measure should be construed as a social measure. In my opinion it is just as much a service measure, a pension
War Veterans Allowance Act

arrangement for the incapacitated veteran as the Pension Act itself.
There is another point I wish to make with regard to permissible earnings under the war veterans allowance arrangement. The veteran now makes $40 a month and of course the $10 a month supplementary is contingent upon a means test. Most of these old soldiers will qualify under that means test, but I think it is wrong to have every recipient of the war veterans allowance in Canada make application for that $10. It should have been automatic, and there should be no means test attached to it. However I leave that to the veterans affairs committee.
I think I am safe in saying that, in 70 per cent of the cases where a man is on war veterans allowance, the permissible earnings of $250 in the case of a single man, and $375 in the case of a married man, do not come into the picture at all. First, in order to qualify for the war veterans allowance you must prove that you are totally unemployable and you must get a medical certificate to that effect. If the doctor certifies that you are totally unemployable and you qualify for the war veterans allowance you are not working and therefore you are not earning an income for the reason that you are not able to do so. You may be able to get a job around Ottawa running an elevator or as a doorman in a hotel, but in most provinces there is not that kind of opportunity open to these men.
For that reason I think I am safe in saying that 70 per cent of the recipients of war veterans allowance are not affected at all by the permissible income and the only income which they have is $30.41 a month. Working it out, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre showed that it was $1,105 and $615, but he is in error because, in the large majority of cases, there is nothing coming in by way of additional income.
In my opinion the demand is reasonable that this should be brought up to $50 a month where a man qualifies as being totally unemployable, worn out and so on, and it should be without a means test. That $50 a month should be applied across the board. Someone may say that is a lot of money, that it costs money. I do not think money should be the determining factor. It was not during the war when there was no difficulty in getting money.
During the war everyone in this house agreed that whatever was physically possible could be made financially possible, and the minister of reconstruction could say, "I am going to build a munitions plant in Quebec. It will cost $25,000,000, but we have the material and the men and here is the money".

Where has all that money gone to? Why quibble about money in a matter of this kind? Every time you put extra money in the hands of a person who is not in a position to contribute to the national income by way of production, every time you put a dollar in his hands he spends it on the essentials of life, and thereby you are creating an internal consuming market which keeps the wheels of industry moving as it supplies that person with those necessities.
For that reason alone, I think we should forget this business about what it will cost the country. I do not think the taxpayers will quibble about it, and I do not think anyone in this house will quarrel if the minister comes and says that he is going to step up the amount to $50 a month without a means test attached to it. If that were done, the old soldier would be happy and he would have some purchasing power. That would stimulate the machinery of production and everybody would be just as happy as the soldier. Why, therefore, quarrel about this business of money? I suggest that we should forget that completely or at least revise our thinking on it to a considerable extent.
There is another problem, namely, that of the veteran and his wife, who by economic circumstances, have been forced to separate. The last time the veterans affairs committee was sitting, I brought to its attention some specific cases. One was that of an old man and his wife receiving war veterans allowance, with married status. The house they were in was sold. They were not in a position to get another one. The father went to live with a daughter and I think the mother went to live with a son; but force of economic circumstances separated them. Immediately that happened, the married status was taken from them. The old lady was left with nothing and the old gentleman's pension was cut down to that of a single man.

That matter was raised in the veterans affairs committee. At that time I suggested that at least some administrative latitude should be given to the board where there were extenuating circumstances of that kind. Nevertheless, no amendments were made. That injustice still exists and I think it should be removed.
In dealing with the pension commission and with the administration of the war veterans allowance, both provincially and nationally,
I have found them to be most sympathetic and reasonable, prepared to do anything they could within the confines of the regulations; but they are tied up by red tape. When I

War Veterans Allowance Act
hear people criticizing the pension commission and war veterans allowance administration, I know that such criticism is unjust. I know that it cannot be justified on the basis of my dealings with them. I know they are sitting there wishing and hoping that the members of the House of Commons had the courage of their convictions and would sit in a committee, prepare an act that was fair, reason- able and just and give it to them to administer. I think they would be quite happy to cure some of the ills that exist in the machinery of the pension administration. As for myself, I think it is too hidebound. I believe that in borderline cases such as that of this old lady and gentleman who were separated, through no fault of their own, the chairman of the commission should have administrative latitude to make a decision, and not allow to take place an injustice such as the separating of a man and his wife and the penalizing of them by the loss of a certain amount of their pension.

The first was with regard to the veteran in the United States who is being discriminated against, in my opinion; and second, with regard to the possibility of separating man and wife because of economic circumstances. I think those two points should be clearly cleaned up in this session of the veterans affairs committee. I also think they should try to give the pension commission and the war veterans allowance board some administrative latitude in borderline cases. Everything cannot be covered. I have some respect for their judgment, and I am quite willing to trust them with many matters that cannot be set down in legislation. I hope the committee will remember that. speechtext:
I shall follow, Mr. Speaker, the good example set by previous speakers and shall also be brief. I first wish to make reference to a remark made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I must thank him kindly for his reference to me. I was perhaps the first to bring in the question of the non-pensioned widows' troubles into the house. As time went on, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and many others strongly endorsed the proposal, and in the end the minister sympathetically put through legislation in favour of the non-pensioned widows. When the matter comes before the committee, and it is an excellent one consisting entirely of war veterans, I hope that further consideration will be given to the non-pensioned widows, to start with.
When I was home two days ago I went to see a war veteran's widow. She was an old lady, living up in a back room in the north end of the riding represented by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey). She is quite an old lady, all crippled up with arthritis. I believe she draws $30.41 a month. She has no relations or no one to assist her in any way. The room was cold. I said to myself that it did not seem quite natural that any human being should be asked to exist-and that is all she can do-on $30.41 a month, after having given her husband in the service of the country. That lady is only one out of many.
I went to see a gentleman who is also a war veterans allowance recipient. It is necessary for him to go to the hospital in Toronto every week in order to receive injections of one kind or another. I believe he has anaemia. He can hardly keep body and soul together with what he receives. If it were not for the fact that his wife also draws a pension, as he is married, he would not be able to make ends meet at all. So I hope and trust that the committee-all of whose members are sympathetic men; and the minister also is most sympathetic with regard to veterans affairs-will see to it that some improvement in their situation is given to both the war veterans and the non-pensioned widows, because this consideration applies in the case of both. They are all thirty years older since the first great war ended and they are that much less capable of earning anything. Furthermore, it is out of the question for them to earn anything at the moment because there has been a big drop in the demand for labour; and that trend, I am sorry to say, is increasing daily. Unless they are given some consideration, their situation will be pitiable.
There is another class of war veteran about whom I wish to say just a word, and that is the South African war veteran. When the estimates for the department come in, I shall have a great deal more to say in that regard. I have in mind a South African war veteran who is now sixty-six or sixty-seven years of age and who, when he went to South Africa, was a mere lad. Of course his body could not have been at that time as well nourished
War Veterans Allowance Act

as it should have been to stand the onslaught of South African diseases, with the result that all his life he has been more or less handicapped but not enough to be knocked out completely. Of late, however, he has been. I have been doing my best to see that that poor fellow gets a square deal, but I have not yet been able to get it for him, merely because his wife happens to have a small income of a few hundred dollars a year. I do not think it is any of the government's business what income the wife of a war veteran may have, particularly when it is a small one like that. He should be treated as we expected he would be treated when the South African pension bill was brought into the house-and I was one of those who advocated that years ago-and that is on his own merits. It is wholly unfair and un-British, to my mind, to say that a man may not receive a small pension merely because his wife has a few hundred dollars a year coming in. So I hope the committee will also take that class of veteran into consideration when it considers this bill.
In the main I think we Canadians may be fairly proud of what our government has done for the war veterans. I do not hear much complaint from the men who served in the front line, the men who were incapacitated or wounded. It is only these complementary offshoots that appear to be giving us trouble these days. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) mentioned another class of which my riding has a large number, though perhaps I should not say more than his; in any event mine is one of the ridings in Canada with a very large number of imperial veterans. In my opinion their treatment has always been very unfair, and I endorse what was said by the hon. member. I need not deal further with this point at the moment, because I want to conclude shortly, and the hon. member put the case so well I could not add anything if I tried. However, I should like hon. members to keep in mind that these men and women are now thirty years older than when world war I ended, and it is these for whom I am speaking in particular.
I think perhaps with a reference to one other class I shall conclude. I have in mind the "Overseas firefighters". I believe the chief came from the riding of the Deputy Speaker, but by far the majority of the "Overseas firefighters" came from the city I represent, and I well remember what they were promised by the minister of that day. They seem to have had quite a difficult time trying to get fair play, and I hope the committee will give consideration to this class of veteran also. They took all the chances anyone else took. It is

true they did not have to go across the channel, but during the last war it was just about as bad in England as on the continent, because of the bombs.
I shall conclude by saying that I always appreciate the opportunity to say a word for the veterans because, as is well known, the riding of Davenport is almost made up of soldiers and their families. They are patriots; and I hope the government and particularly the minister will listen to the representations which will be made on their behalf to the committee to which this bill is to be sent.
