speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no criticism of the minister or the cabinet, but as a veteran of the first war I wish to say a word on behalf of the veterans. I have in mind an expression which I would direct to the veterans affairs committee and to the minister, in the hope that he will go to the cabinet and have this bill reconsidered. Those words are: "Lest we forget." Many of us do not realize that the soldier has been a terrific factor in building up this great country. In 1812 the habitant said, "By gar, I guess that Yankee is going to take our country," and the Englishman said, "By Jove, that shan't be," and the two of them worked together on the St. Lawrence to defend this country. So today it is possible for us to sit in this House of Commons and discuss what is the fair thing to do for our ex-soldiers.
All of us in the house can think back to when we were boys and we heard of the great deeds performed by our soldiers in the South African war. How proud we were to welcome them back, and how in our hearts we felt an obligation to those men who returned wearing their scarlet coats. I was a little boy in the town of Rat Portage, which is now Kenora. I was really too young to understand what these veterans were, but I knew they were coming home and I was proud to be there to welcome them back. We think back also to August 4, 1914, when some person attempted to twist the lion's tail. Again the oldest cub in the pack stood beside the mother country without hesitation. They doubted whether this country would be able to raise the first division of thirty thousand men, but the number volunteering was greater than the number requested by England or offered by Canada. Soon 31,000 men sailed from the shores of Canada as the first contingent, perfectly equipped and ready to fight, and those men made history. Again in 1939 war was forced upon this country, and again men volunteered to fight for their homes and their freedom.
Today we are in parliament, dealing in a somewhat niggardly fashion with these men;

War Veterans Allowance Act
and this is the only place to which these veterans can appeal for fair treatment. Again I remind the government of the words: "Lest we forget." Think of the times during the first great war when our men trudged up to the trenches, with the rain pouring off their steel helmets and the mud soaking their shoes; drenched to the skin, standing in the trenches for three or four days at a time, then going out to wooden huts poorly heated and equipped. Today many of those veterans who returned from that war without a wound find that, on account of the conditions under which they served their country they need aid from this parliament. So I say to the members of the veterans affairs committee, to the minister and to the cabinet: Do not think you are overly generous if you deal honestly and reasonably with these people.
Fortunately I am not myself in need of a pension. Though I did suffer wounds during the first war I have enjoyed good health since; but I speak on behalf of the man who was disabled in the war, or who has suffered some mental defect, or who, because of the conditions under which he fought, now finds it necessary to come and say to his fellow countrymen, "Give me a helping hand." I say to the members of this house, do not look at the men who have preserved this country for us as you would look at anyone or anything else in this country. Lean backward in your attempt to be overly generous to them. No right-thinking man in this country will criticize you; or if such men do, their criticism is not worth considering.
I say, take this bill back; cut out the means test for these veterans; make it unnecessary for any veteran to have to appeal for a $10 increase. Be men about it. This country owes it to them. I owe dt to them; you owe it to them. Remember that phrase "Lest we forget." It is so easy to forget what our soldiers have meant to Canada. Because of them it is possible for us to sit here today and listen to the arguments advanced on behalf of these men; but we also have to listen to instances which should never have occurred and should never have to be cited in this house. The veterans affairs department and the dominion government have a duty to perform. I ask them to perform that duty dn such a way that in future we shall not have to listen to cases such as we have heard cited during this debate. They are not justifiable; they are unreasonable; they are not fair to the men who have made it possible for us to sit here in peace and safety.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words with respect to this War Veterans Allowance Act, by
reason of the fact that I spoke on the Pension Act when it was in the resolution stage and I now find it necessary to augment what I said at that time. It will be recalled that I advocated something I do not believe had been advocated before. I urged that veterans who had seen actual warfare should be paid a pension, regardless of anything else. I also made the suggestion that no member of His Majesty's armed forces who had been in an actual theatre of war should be now compelled to pay taxes, due to the fact that most of our tax money is for the retirement of the war debt. Our men in the forces should not be asked to fight the war and then, upon their return, be asked to help pay for it.
The reason I mention this the second time is that, when I spoke before, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) followed me in the debate and suggested to the house that what I had urged was not sound. That took place before the Easter recess. Since that time I have received a considerable volume of correspondence, some from individuals and some from veterans organizations, complimenting me upon the stand I took at that time. So I do not believe that what I said was so unsound as the hon. member for Kootenay West would have led the house to believe.
While I do not intend to take up much time in debate because, as I understand it, the bill is to be sent to the veterans affairs committee, I would ask if it is possible to have information as to the basis upon which the present pension rates are arrived at. In other words, why should the full pension be estimated at the sum of $87. Why should it not be $100 or $150? Or, on the other hand, why should it be as high as $87? Why should it not be $50? Just what is the reason for setting it at $87? There must be some basis of calculation; there must be some reason for the amount as it now stands. By what means does the government arrive at that figure? Does it base the figure on the cost of living? Does it estimate that, because the cost of living is related to a certain index, therefore the pension is $87? Is that the way it is done? Or has it arrived at that figure by taking out pencil and paper and estimating that the average income per person in the country is so much, and that therefore the pension should be $87? Is that the way it is estimated? I wonder what the basis of calculation might be; I have not been able to arrive at it.

speechtext:
I plead for better consideration of our war veterans. But I wish to emphasize particularly that part of the bill which has to do with allowances given to veterans who are not pensioned, and to the widows of non-pensioned war veterans.
There are some peculiar anomalies in this whole scheme of war veterans allowances. For instance, let me give an illustration. I have in mind two widows of war veterans who live in the same district and not far from each other. One of these widows, whom we shall call Mrs. X, receives a pension of $60 a month by reason of the fact that her husband was a war pensioner. He did not see an actual theatre of war, and was never sent overseas. For some reason or another he received the pension. It may have been because of a condition of health due to war service. This bill will increase the pension of Mrs. X to $70 a month.
The other widow, whom we shall designate as Mrs. Y, lives not far from the first one. The husband of Mrs. Y was sent overseas, served in an actual theatre of war and returned safe and sound. Eventually he took ill and found himself without income. He applied for assistance under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and received it. He had been in receipt of that assistance for only a few months when he died, leaving his widow penniless. Of course she was then entitled to an allowance. At the present time she receives the full allowance of $30.41.
This widow, Mrs. Y, has a heart ailment and is unable to work and thus augment her war widow's allowance. As I said, these two war widows live in the same district and move in the same social circle, if I might use that terminology as applying to them. I should like to know why one of these women is entitled to a higher standard of living than the other. I cannot understand why the difference exists. I think there is some reason for our asking for reconsideration of this scheme of war veterans allowances for widows of our veterans.
I should like to make a suggestion. Many of these widows in receipt of allowances are under the impression that they are receiving a pension. It is difficult sometimes to explain to them that it is an allowance rather than a pension they are receiving, that they are receiving an allowance because of their financial circumstances. I do not like to say it

when I am explaining it to them, but I can say to the minister, and I think he will agree with me, that what these war widows are really receiving under this act is relief. That is what it amounts to.
There is just a slight difference between their case and the old-fashioned dishing out of relief. When we were on relief we had to go down to the city office every Thursday or whatever day or hour might be set and stand in line. We presented our identification cards and were given a slip of paper entitling us to so much groceries from this store, milk from this dairy and our rent.

speechtext:
I am glad to hear the minister say that. I am glad to hear him say that he considers there is no difference. I do. The only difference is that the war widow in receipt of a war widow's allowance gets her cheque every month. She does not have to be embarrassed by going down to an office to get it and she can spend it in any way she wishes. I think I am right in that diagnosis.
Another thing in this bill I want to protest about is the means test which is applied to widows receiving this war veterans allowance. I protest against the means test in any event, but I protest especially this second means test. Under this measure, if there is to be an increase in the allowance it is subject to the board, and I take that to mean that there must be a reinvestigation of the widow's circumstances. Surely if her circumstances have been investigated once and she is in receipt of a war widow's allowance, the increase should be automatic.
Some of the previous speakers have deplored the pittance that is given under this bill, and I do thh same. In some respects I sympathize with the minister because I know that he would like to make the amount far greater than it is. I know that personally he would like to put the pensions up as far as it is possible to go, and also the war widows' allowances. But I know that he is subject to government policy. I know that in whatever he says under the bill he must protect the policy of the government. There is no getting away from that, and it is the government policy that I am now attacking because the provisions made by this bill are inadequate for these pensioners and especially for war widows who are left penniless.

War Veterans Allowance Act
I am reminded of a gentleman, not a war pensioner, who died not so long ago. He was a millionaire who had been one of the leading restauranteurs in the United States. He made so much money in the restaurant business that he went insane and he died in an insane asylum. He died crying out, "Cut the ham thinner, boys; cut the ham thinner." It appears to me that perhaps the government is on its last legs. This would seem to be so from what it has been responsible for recently. There has been the income tax forms, a reluctance to make any change in freight rates and so on. Surely the government is facing the insane asylum and now, by this bill, is crying out, "Cut the ham thinner, boys; cut the ham thinner".

I have said what I wanted to say. I believe that our veterans, and especially their widows, should be treated as this country can afford to treat them. I do not mean afford by virtue of the amount of taxes the finance minister can squeeze out of the public. I mean what we can afford to give them by reason of our vast wealth, and no one will say that this country is not one of the richest in the world. It is up to the government, therefore, to adjust its policies so as to make that wealth available to the people and especially to war
veterans and widows of war veterans who are called upon in these days of high cost of living to live on a mere pittance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that has just been made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) that veterans should not pay taxes is one that I believe will not be well received by a great many veterans in this country. The men who volunteered and went overseas and fought to defend this country and overcome the forces of evil are, I believe, just as anxious to bear their full share of the responsibilities of this country in peace as in war.

They believe they should bear their full responsibility and pay their full share as citizens of this country. I believe that the majority of the members of the Canadian Legion, as it is usually referred to, though its full name is the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League-and I must say I like that name and am proud of it-want to serve their country as faithfully and loyally in peace as they did in war.
I rise, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of making one suggestion only, and I shall be very brief. I am not a member of the committee to which this bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act is to be referred, and my purpose in rising is to ask that committee to amend the bill to provide a veterans allowance for those men who volunteered for service in the Boer war and went to South Africa but did not arrive there until January 1, 1902. It was not their fault that the war came to an end before they engaged the enemy. They volunteered for service and went overseas, as did the men in the second great war who are to be granted this allowance because they went to Great Britain. But, as I understand the act. the men I speak of who went to South Africa and arrived there after January 1, 1902. are not eligible for the veterans allowance. These men are now old, and many of them are not capable of doing the work they formerly did. Some of them are in need of assistance. If this act is to be regarded as a social security measure, as some members who have taken part in the debate have said, every consideration should be given to these men and they should be granted the veterans allowance.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) on the second reading of the bill informed the house that only 592 veterans of the South African war were in receipt of this allowance. If the act were amended to include the men who went to South Africa

but did not arrive there before January 1, 1902, the additional number would not be large and their inclusion would involve no great strain on the treasury of this country. So I would ask the committee when the bill comes before it to amend it by providing that men who volunteered for service in the South African war and who went to South Africa but did not arrive there before January 1, 1902, be included among those who are entitled to a veterans allowance.

Bell Telephone Company
The house resumed from Friday, March 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Rinfret for the second reading of Bill No. 8, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on this bill, and first of all I should like to refresh the memories of hon. members by referring to the explanatory note. The purpose of this bill is to obtain authority to increase the capital stock of the company from $150 million to S500 million. The company's present authorized capital stock is $150 million. There remains yet unissued $13,336,700 of authorized capital stock. So far there has been no adequate explanation of this tremendous increase in capital stock.
At this point I think I ought to express my personal appreciation of the efforts of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and other hon. members who have taken part in this debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Good public ownership members.

Yes. I congratulate them on the good service which I believe they have rendered to this house and to the country by taking the attitude they have toward this legislation.
I recall that in 1928 this company appeared before parliament for an increase in its capital by S75,000.000, and at that time there was as keen opposition as there is on this occasion to permitting the company to increase its stock to the extent then proposed, the only difference being that at that time there was more strenuous opposition to the manner in which the company had been accustomed to . issue its stock.
At that time there were charges that the company had issued its stock to its friends, to members of the company. It issued new stock at par to the members of the company, while the value of the stock was as high as $193.
I was looking up the old records here in the 1928 Hansard, at page 3084, and I find a quotation from the Toronto Globe of that time of a statement made by a Mr. Reid, who was counsel for the province of Ontario before the railway commission when the matter of telephone rates was up for discussion. Speaking of the Bell Telephone Company at that time, that gentleman made this statement:
The history of its stock issues shows that the company has been making a regular practice of issuing stock to it shareholders at par of $100 per share when it was listed and selling on the
exchanges at market prices, forty per cent, fifty per cent, sixty per cent, seventy-five per cent, and in the instance in the year 1899 at ninety-three per cent higher than its par value, and in each of such cases the shareholders were given a bonus of $49, $47, $50, $60, $75 and $93 per share, in addition to the regular dividend of eight per cent.
That was a very fair melon, if you like to call it that, and I imagine that the taste is still keen for that kind of fruit. It is just possible that with $500 million capitalization there would be afforded an opportunity for carloads of such melons to be brought in.
Don't you like melons?

I do not like melons, if my hon. friend wants to know. As a matter of fact I usually get lemons, and my hon. friend is probably in the same boat. However, this telephone business is one of those services which I think most people will agree should be under public ownership. The telephone system should be run, if any service is run, for the purpose of giving the utmost service to the community at large and not for any profit whatsoever. It should be run at cost, at the cost of maintaining the service. I know of no other way by which proper services can be given to all the people impartially.
A private company running a telephone system for the profits which it can make from the enterprise will invariably centre its services in the larger communities and sometimes neglect entirely the sparsely settled communities. In this bill there is absolutely no provision for any extension of service to be rendered to the public. No assurance is given in the bill anywhere that under certain conditions the company will be obligated to give service to the community, and until such assurance is absolutely guaranteed I certainly think we would be remiss in our duty if we passed this measure.
The last time the bill was before the house some hon. member-I am not sure who it was but I believe it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-suggested that the more people there were on a telephone line, the more expensive it was. That, of course, is not true. It is true, I think, that the more people there are on the telephone system, the better the service or at least the greater service one gets for the money paid for the telephone because he is put in touch with a greater number of people. But I think the minister would not hold that, if half the people of Ottawa had their telephones cut off tomorrow, the other half would get their telephones much
Bell Telephone Company

cheaper because of that. Yet that would be the logic of the point of view which was then expressed.
It depends on the number of lines.

I am opposed to this bill and I am opposed to the increase in capitalization, first, because I am opposed to giving a monopoly of a public service of this kind to any company whatsoever. No private company is good enough to be trusted with a monopoly of a public service. So from that point of view I wish to register my objection. It is not only the fact that this company has the monopoly of the telephone business in eastern Canada, but through its subsidiary, the Northern Electric Company, it has also practically the control of all supplies necessary for the telephone systems throughout the country. If I remember rightly, the point was brought out in discussion in 1928 that this Bell Telephone Company would buy its supplies from itself at enormous prices, and thus make profits through its own subsidiary in a manner which could not have happened had there been any competition at all in supplying the requirements of the company. In other words, it could over-charge itself through its own subsidiary, and the public paid the difference in charges made for services.
As I say, there has been no explanation of this over-capitalization of $500,000,000, and no satisfactory explanation has been offered to the house as to why this should be asked for or why it should be granted. This, however, we can say. The public, in the last analysis, must pay for all capitalization; and particularly will it be required to pay for over-capitalization. So I would remind the sponsor of this bill that I for one wish to have a more complete explanation of why this increase in capital is being asked for, and I also want-
Let it go to the committee, then.

-to know how the stock is to be issued. My hon. friend says to let it go to the committee. By that he means, let us first get the endorsement of the house to something that we do not like; then when we get to the committee we shall be told that the principle of the bill has already been passed, and to take it and like it.
That is not so with regard to private bills.

That is the way things go. I do not propose just to let things go to a committee without offering my objection beforehand, so that I may be sure that I have had

an opportunity of making that objection. Perhaps the most objectionable feature of the bill is the stock-splitting proposal, and that will be found in the third section of the bill.
Order.
I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that I am not supposed to quote from the bill.
Order. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the general principle of the bill. The section of the bill.may be dealt with when we reach the committee stage.
Not 10 per cent.
I do not like that hypocritical way of doing the thing. I think this company should be required to face up-
In dollars; not in percentage.
I think my hon. friend is getting warm, as we say in the old game.

"Exasperated" is the word.

It is quite true that it does not alter the actual profits that might be made.
Why does the hon. member not say what he means?
But it alters the report of that profit. That is the thing I am trying to get at.
It does not alter the profits at all.

My hon. friend may take the floor, or whatever you want to call it, and 6ay all he wants to say when I am through. I am expressing what appears to me to be the situation, or a possible situation to be brought about by the splitting of stock. If it cannot be so, and my hon. friend can show that, I shall be glad to learn it. But I am not the only one who takes that view. I can show my hon. friend, or quote to my hon. friend the words of men of financial repute in this city and in the employ of this government, which would support the point I am making there, and show that they say exactly the same thing about it that I have just said.
The next abjection to the splitting of the stock is that usually those who buy later on are at a disadvantage, for this reason. Of course the excuse is always, "Oh, we split the stock because we want the dear public all to come in."
The widows and orphans.

Yes. It is easier for them to buy a $25 share than a $100 share; so it is said, "It is in the interests of the dear people that we are splitting our stock". I know that is the excuse, but this is what usually follows. When stock is split in this fashion there is usually a quickening of the market, a stimulation, so the stock goes up. The original $100 share may be split into four $25 shares, and each of those shares may go from $25 to $30.
Time to sell.

Well, if it goes up to $30 it has greatly benefited the original stockholders. But then they begin to unload on, shall I say, the suckers; is that a parliamentary word? That is where they unload it; the dear people become suckers and pay the extra stock values that their own competition to get in on the cheap stock has created. That is the usual practice in a stock-splitting proposition of this kind. The $25 share may go up to $30. It may go twice as high, but let us say it goes to $30. This increases the original value from $100 to $120, which is a very considerable
increase for those who have the privilege of holding the original stock. As I say, the newcomers take the loss; the original shareholders make the gain, and in the last analysis I presume the public pays.
The next principle in this bill to which I object is that which gives this company the right to deal in or control wireless and radio and all the newest devices, appliances and principles which may be developed in these matters. I cannot quote this, but it is stated in the bill that this is a clarification of powers the company has always had. If the company has always had them, what is the need of clarification? But if the company did not always have them the clarification, so called, will see that it gets them from now on. So I am opposed to that provision in this bill. Surely this house is of the opinion by now that wireless, radio, television and so on should not be entrusted to any private corporation. No private company, I repeat, should be given power to handle a public service such as radio communication, television and so on.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this bill. My hon. friend may think I am going to try to talk out the bill. I am not. I am going to conclude my remarks right now, because I want every measure to have an opportunity to be voted upon in this house. I do not believe it would be democratic for me or anyone else to occupy all the time available to this or any other bill in order to prevent it from coming to a vote in the house. I have, however, taken this opportunity to register my protest, and if others feel like it I hope that they will do the same; that ultimately this legislation will come to a vote, and that the house will vote it down.

Since the introduction of this bill I have become very much interested in the action that probably will be taken should it pass the house. I have discovered that the Bell Telephone monopoly is one of the largest monopolies in existence anywhere in the world; and I think it would pay all hon. members to read one of the books in our parliamentary library which deals with this Bell monopoly. It is entitled: "The American Telegraph and Telephone Company; the Story of a Great Monopoly", by Horace Coon, and was written in 1939. It is absolutely amazing the number of companies controlled by the American Telegraph and Telephone Company, and I should like to give a list of at least some of these corporations. At page 155 of this book I find that these associated companies are controlled by the Bell system in the United States-
Bell Telephone Company
What about Canada?

The system in Canada is controlled by the same company in the United States, and they also control the English telephone system. Take the New England Telegraph and Telephone Company; 66-31 per cent of its stock is controlled by the company I have mentioned.
Order. If I understand the hon. member correctly he is about to quote a number of companies who are affiliated with the Bell Telephone Company of the United States?
Yes.
The bill before the house is not concerned with the Bell Telephone Company of the United States; it has to do with the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

I agree entirely, Mr. Speaker, but I think it can be easily seen by all hon. members that since the Bell system in Canada is only a part of the American system it is relevant to point out that this is one great world monopoly in the field of telephone communication.

Order. The hon. member knows perfectly well that on second reading the debate should be confined to the principle of the bill which is before the house. The bill under consideration just now is with respect to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. So I would ask the hon. member who has the floor and other hon. members to confine their remarks to the merits of the bill before the house.

If I may comment on the point of order, this bill asks for the extension of the capital of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and surely anything bearing upon that has to do with the principle of the bill. You cannot discuss the principle of the bill without associating it with something else. So I should say the remarks of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Moore) are quite in order and that it has always been in order to discuss a matter of this kind.

I am sorry, but I do not agree with the hon. gentleman. It is clear that the bill before the house has to do with the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, so the hon. member should confine his remarks to that company.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not entirely agree that these other matters should not be considered in connection with the Canadian system. However, since it is the

ruling of the Chair that what I have been saying is out of order with respect to this bill I shall confine my remarks to the Bell system in Canada. At the start I want to say that I am not in any way attacking the Bell system for its labour relations or any matters of that kind. I believe we have to concede right at the beginning that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is one of the best private companies in this country for which any individual could wish to work. But the principle behind this bill is not in the interest of the public -of Canada. And I venture to say that, instead of this house passing the legislation, we ought to look to the time when we in Canada shall be able to control our telephone system. Already we control it in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and some of the other western provinces. The reason we control it there is that at the time telephone lines were built in western Canada it was not profitable to go into that business. I believe that, particularly in Manitoba, it began as private enterprise but, to use a common term, it fell through, and the government had to take it over.
That is not true.
The government took it over anyway.
It took it over, but it was not broke.
It was very nearly.
Badly cracked.
The same position as the five privately owned railroads.
Not at all.

Otherwise private enterprise would not have allowed it to be taken over. The only reason we have this great monopoly today is that it was profitable at that time to go into that business.
There was only one other point I wished to make this evening in connection with this telephone system. There is great danger that if we continue the private ownership of telephone systems in Ontario and Quebec they will in time control radio broadcasting as well. Here again we find a similarity with the position in the United States. At page 205 of this informative book it states:
The Bell system has a stranglehold on the radio industry at one of that industry's most strategic and vulnerable points, for it has a virtual monopoly in furnishing the wire facilities to broadcasting stations. Chain or network broadcasting cannot be made in the United States without the use of Bell system wires.

Bell Telephone Company
I submit that if we continue to allow the private ownership of telephones to expand in Canada we may get in this respect a similar situation in connection with radio to that now existing in the United States. I intend to vote against this measure.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker
When do we get this vote?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member asks when we shall vote. If I have anything to say about the matter, we shall vote in a very few minutes.
We will let you help your friends in a minute.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We of this group have made clear our position on the bill. We are not alone; we have had the excellent support of my good friend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and my good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), as well as the support of a few other public ownership members of the Tory party.
The basic reason for our objection to the bill is that we see in it the strengthening of a private monopoly in connection with a public service. Like my two good friends in the front row of the Tory party, here-
Oh, talk for yourself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Take all the time you want. We feel that a public service of this kind should be a public monopoly and that we should move in that direction rather than in the direction of strengthening a private monopoly. In addition to that fundamental objection to the bill, we feel that even those in the house who do not support public ownership still have a responsibility to the people of Canada, whom they represent to consider a bill like this most carefully before it is passed. In the main-
Let it go to the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If my hon. friend will contain himself for a moment I shall make a suggestion which will be helpful.
We are talking.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Now, where was I, before the Minister of Labour's voice distracted my attention?
You were against giving greater monopoly to private enterprise. That is the one point, sum and substance of all your speeches.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Well, I am delighted to learn we have been able to make our point sufficiently clear that the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) understands it. That is a feather in the cap of the C.CE.
Don't be so ungentlemanly as to be boring.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was endeavouring to point out that even private ownership members in the house should look several times before they approve the principle of a bill which contains two particularly offensive features. One of those features is what we regard as a tremendous increase in the authorized capitalization; the other feature we regard as offensive is the one to which my colleague from Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) referred, namely the giving of retroactive rights in the field of radio, television and other things mentioned in the bill.
I feel there are members in the house who do not go along with us so far as our public ownership views are concerned, but who nevertheless consider that to grant this sort of extension of privilege to private interests is not good for private enterprise itself. It is just this sort of thing, as some private enterprise supporters realize, that brings private enterprise into disrepute.
For these reasons it seems to me that the discussion of the proposed legislation in committee, which the hon. member sponsoring the bill is so anxious to have, should take place before approval is given to the principle of the bill. The hon. member for Cariboo has already answered one interjection on that point by indicating what usually happens. Once second reading has been voted, we are told that from then on the house has approved the bill in principle, and that there is nothing left to do but to talk about minor details and, in the end, the bill becomes law.
So, as a generous gesture to the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) who wishes to get this matter to committee, and so as to facilitate the taking of the vote other hon. members have asked for, I move in amendment seconded by my deskmate, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson):
That Bill No. 8, letter C of the senate, be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion? Those in favour of the motion will say "yea".
Yea.

Those opposed will say "Nay".
Bell Telephone Company
Nay.

In my opinion the "nays"
have it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You wanted a vote.
We asked for bread and he gave us a stone.

Mr. Speaker, it was our hope that this bill would have been allowed to go to a committee where all the relevant facts in regard to the company could have been brought out; but, since this is not to be done, it is not my intention to see the vote taken on the second reading until we know more about the principle of the measure.
How are you going to find out?

If the bill had been sent to a committee we could have got the facts with regard to this application and the need for this increased capitalization.
First, let me say that if the bill related only to telephone service we might have let it pass, but it seeks to raise the authorized capital stock of the company from 8150,000,000 to 8500.000,000, which would make the company of such magnitude that it would affect the living and well-being of a great many Canadian people. This company has extended its service in the eastern part of Canada to the point where today it is practically a monopoly. Were that the only thing implied by this bill, it would not be too bad, but obviously we are on the eve of great developments in the field of communication.
Order. The hour for private bills having expired, the house will now revert to the business before it at six o'clock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gregg for the second reading of Bill No. 196, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner hour the members of the house were expressing their views on the principle of the amendments to Bill No. 196, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. As I said when I rose to my feet at six o'clock, since I am not

War Veterans Allowance Act
privileged to act on the veterans affairs committee this year, I should like to mention a number of deficiencies in the bill for consideration by the committee.
First of all, I share the feeling expressed by other hon. members that the amounts allowed to those veterans who are unfortunate enough to require the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act are insufficient under present circumstances. The bill as it stands gives a maximum contribution from government sources, to the participants of the benefits of the legislation, of $40 a month for single persons or $70 a month for married persons, and there are permitted certain additional small incomes from other sources. The over-all effect is, of course, unchanged from the previous years. The total permissible income in the case of single veterans is $615 a year, and in the case of married veterans, $1,105 a year.
In view of the increase in the cost of living in the last couple of years particularly, in which we have had a rise in two years of 30 points, the minister might well have considered a bonus, perhaps on a sliding scale, in addition to whatever his government felt was a proper base income-a sliding scale bonus which would go up and down on the basis of the rise or fall in the cost of living, from a certain well defined yardstick, whether it be the scale of 1939 or the scale applying at the end of hostilities. A base period might well have been considered for which the allowance as it is now written into the proposed act might apply, -with supplements that would vary periodically with the rise and fall in the cost of living.
There is one further deficiency that I see. I feel that the minister might have considered at the same time including in this war veterans allowance legislation the right of the veteran to receive certain specified medical treatment and hospitalization. That might be included to supplement further the benefits which the veteran might receive from the legislation, because, in the case of the married veteran receiving somewdiat better than $2 a day, if from that sum there must be subtracted the cost of unforeseen accident or illness, with hospitalization and the medical bills that would ensue, he is worse off than the destitute, after all is said and done.
When the minister gave his statement yesterday he informed the house that there were under 31,000 recipients of benefits from the act-30,949, if his figures are correct, and I will question one phase of that in a moment- with a total cost to the Canadian nation of just under $15,000,000 as of the year 1947- $14,952,000 odd.
I think there may be one error in this statement and I should like the minister to make a note of it and to explain the figures as he has them. For example, under the heading "orphans, all wars", he told the house that there were fifty-three recipients of benefits and that the total liability on an annual basis was $25,596. That amounts to nearly $500 per orphan on an annual basis. The minister will concede that, according to the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946, which is not amended in this particular under part II of the act, under clause 8, subsection 3, the maximum allowance payable in any year to or on behalf of orphan or orphans shall be $360 in the case of one child, and so on, and there is a sliding scale downwards. So that I think the minister should give some explanation with respect to that figure on the basis of $360 per orphan. The liability for fifty-three orphans would be something in the neighbourhood of $19,000 instead of $25,000. Unquestionably, therefore, there is an error either in the amount or in the number of recipients. Perhaps the fifty-three refers to fifty-three families of recipients. I trust the minister will give an explanation in that regard.
Another point which I think the minister should consider is with respect to the present amount payable under the War Veterans Allowance Act. This corresponds so nearly to the amounts that are payable by way of old age pensions in certain provinces, when the dominion does in fact pay the maximum, that it may under certain circumstances be desirable for the recipient of the war veterans allowance to refuse to accept the allowance and to accept the old age pension of the province.
I know it is not the wish of the Department of Veterans Affairs to increase the fiscal burden of the various provinces by having them assume the cost of the payment of allowances in respect of veterans; but under part IV of the War Veterans Allowance Act, which is not amended by the bill before the house, a recipient of the war veterans allowance cannot accept the old age pension of a province while at the same time accepting the war veterans allowance.
There is another matter I would ask the minister to consider. I believe he can do this with great credit to the department, and it would not cover a large number of cases. According to the present War Veterans Allowance Act, veterans' widows are eligible for pension only when they have attained the age of fifty-five, and then, of course, only under certain circumstances. Widows under fifty-five years of age are not eligible according to the
5849-180i
War Veterans Allowance Act

act, unless permanently unemployable by reason of physical or mental disability. That is the way the act reads.
There are widows in their forties, with children, who are neither physically nor mentally disabled, but because the children are too young, the mothers cannot leave them to find employment. Such widows are unable to qualify for the allowance under this act as it now reads. I am sure the number involved throughout Canada would not be excessive, and in view of the fact that the total cost of the act is not to be stepped up immeasurably as a result of the amendment the minister has brought in-it was under $15,000,000 as of December last-this will not create an additional burden on the dominion treasury, while it will help to rectify a situation which I feel the minister himself and the treasury benches would not wish to see perpetuated.
There is one final consideration, Mr. Speaker, and that is that there is no special provision for children unless they are orphans; that is, unless father and mother are both deceased. There are innumerable cases across this country where the recipient of that allowance has more than one or two children. In fact, it is one of the paradoxes of life, almost, that the more necessitous the circumstances of many people, the larger the family with which they are blessed. For our unfortunate veterans who must apply for war veterans allowance it seems to me that a case could be made out comparable with that for families of pensioners where consideration is paid to the size of the family.
I say, first of all, that I feel the minister has allowed the treasury board to be niggardly in the amount which it is allotting for war veterans allowances generally under present conditions. Because of the similarity in amount of provincial old age pensions and war veterans allowance, I feel there is a danger that there will be a temptation for the veteran in certain provinces to apply for the old age pension-when he reaches the age of seventy, of course-rather than to use the financial resources of the Department of Veterans Affairs for his support. I think the minister should see to it that no injustice is done to the province, and that special provision should be made for widows under the age of fifty-five who have children. In the case of large families, or families with more than one child, I think some supplementary allowance should be paid to the children of such veterans.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to add a word at this time, Mr. Speaker, because I believe there should be evidence of a desire on the part of members generally to encourage

the committee to give more generous consideration to the provisions outlined in this bill. This is a measure introduced by a newcomer to the department., the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg). I think the attitude we take here could encourage him and could strengthen his hand in his appeals to the government to provide more generous treatment for the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I suggest that we cannot afford to be niggardly with these veterans or the veterans' dependents. As a matter of fact we can afford to be generous, when one appreciates the resources of this great nation and the wealth which we possess. I would ask hon. members to recall, if they will, the fact that these veterans played their full part in preserving our way of life, in guaranteeing to us the security which we enjoy today. If we let our minds go back to those trying times when the bands were playing and the soldiers were marching forth to battle, it will be brought home to us that it is a sad commentary that the soldier is the man of the day and the man of the hour, but he is all too soon forgotten.
While these veterans were away, many men who remained at home had an opportunity to augment or to build up their resources. That opportunity was denied to the veteran who was serving overseas. Those years were lost years in the ordinary course of civilian life. The veteran suffered that handicap, if no other. I agree with my hon. friend who spoke this afternoon when he said that the veterans are not seeking any preferred treatment in their status as citizens of this country. They are willing to carry their full share of the load. But I feel that they are entitled to a just and proper reward for meritorious service in the defence of their country, that their widows should have consideration, and that their children particularly should have an opportunity of receiving an education comparable with that received by children of others who have been more fortunate and have been able to provide this opportunity for them.
Unfortunately, the world is a long way from being at peace. Already we hear notes of discord and the distant rumble of warfare. As a matter of fact there are those who will say that we are now at war-a cold war. We may again find it necessary to call upon the manhood of this nation to make a similar sacrifice. It is only fair that those who are prepared to make that contribution should have the absolute assurance that there will be, in reality, a sense of economic security for them. In other words, while we hesitate to glorify war, the present signs indicate that soldiering has become a profession; and it will remain

War Veterans Allowance Act
so as long as the world is in this state of anxiety and as long as this discord and lack of understanding prevail throughout the world. So I submit that our future security and our future ability to encourage another generation, or even this generation, of young men to take up arms, may depend upon the attitude we express in our parliament today.
I consider it most important that the committee on veterans affairs, to whom this bill will be referred, should be encouraged to believe that there is a large degree of unanimity in this house in regard to our desire to see that the veteran and his family receive far more generous treatment than they have received in the past. I can think of young men, now growing older, who, through a sense of loyalty and a sense of devotion, went forth to battle and played a tremendous part, who have since returned to our midst and whose health has been of an indifferent character all these years. They have not had the robust physique which has been enjoyed by some of their more fortunate fellow citizens; thus they have been under a handicap all these years. Now, as the shades of evening come closer, they are met with a degree of adversity, a lack of security; and I certainly feel that a burnt-out veteran and his family should not be subjected to the means test. With our wealth and resources we should indicate to these veterans that the nation is solidly behind them in peace just as we idolized them in war, when our very existence depended upon their bravery and courage.
So I would respectfully submit that the veterans affairs committee should take note of the temper of the speakers who have participated in this debate. They have endeavoured to interpret the attitude of thousands of Canadian people, and to show that the country is prepared to deal generously with her veterans. I believe the minister, who is directly responsible to the veterans, to this house and to the government, should pay heed to the remarks which have been made, because I have not heard one hon. member say this was enough. Everyone has urged more generous treatment. Everyone has intimated that he feels we are being altogether too niggardly. With that expression of opinion, surely the minister can approach his cabinet colleagues determined to secure their support for more adequate treatment of our veterans. With that leadership on the part of the minister and the members of the veterans affairs committee, I sincerely hope that more generous treatment will be given those to whom we owe so much, particularly with respect to economic security for themselves and their families.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any length this evening on this measure because as a member of the veterans affairs committee I shall have an opportunity later to bring up most of the points with which I wish to deal. Since that committee was set up, however, most hon. members of this house as well as the members of that committee have received many letters from veterans and veterans' organizations protesting against the treatment being given the veterans under the various acts. The measure now before the house, the War Veterans Allowance Act, is one of those measures which we think do not meet the requirements of the veterans. I believe every hon. member will agree that a single veteran in receipt of $365 a year, or $30.41 a month, does not receive enough to maintain anything like a Canadian standard of living. It is true, of course, that he is allowed other income up to a total of $615 a year; nevertheless even that is not sufficient to maintain a Canadian standard of living.
The main objection most veterans' organizations have with respect to the government's legislation is that it is not sufficiently generous toward the veterans, and I can wholeheartedly agree with that contention. For example, I do not see why a single veteran should not receive at least $50 and a married man at least $100 a month. I know there are people who argue that such expenditures on behalf of our veterans would take a great deal of money from the treasury. No doubt that is true; but it is also true that the income of this country is higher than ever before in our history. So while the government have this money I think they ought to place legislation on the statute books which will give our veterans a reasonable standard of living.
Then I should like to say a word in support of the veterans of the South African war. I believe this legislation should apply to them as well. There are other things I shall deal with when this matter comes before the veterans affairs committee, but I want to repeat that veterans across this country are not satisfied with the legislation which has been brought down. They feel it is not sufficiently generous, and I think they are right. I do not believe they can maintain anything like a reasonable standard of living on the amounts they receive under the War Veterans Allowance Act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
This may be my only chance to say something in connection with this matter, since I am not on the committee. I shall not detain the house for
War Veterans Allowance Act

long, but I felt it my duty to make a few remarks. I am glad the minister has seen fit to bring down this bill. It is long overdue, but it has been a great disappointment to me, as I am sure it has been to others. In introducing the bill, the minister said, as reported at page 2788 of Hansard:
The terms of this bill will, I anticipate, receive careful study by the special committee on veterans affairs.
I hope it does receive careful study, so much so that when the bill is brought back to the house hon. members may have difficulty in recognizing it. Then the minister went on:
In the main, Mr. Speaker, this bill is a further important step toward giving the old soldier who fought for his country the assurance that in his old age his country will provide him with some defence against poverty.
I do not think the amounts provided under this bill, a maximum of $40 for a single man and $70 for a married man, even with the amounts they are permitted to earn in addition, will give these veterans much protection .against poverty. We must remember that the $20 the old soldier got back in 1930 was worth about $50 in terms of today's values, so that not very much is being given at the present time. I suggest that the minimum should be $50. It is within the discretion of the board to allow $50 in case of need for a single man, and up to $100 in case of need for a married man, but I say these men should be given a chance to earn a much larger total. I believe that total should be $750 for a single man and $1,200 for a married man; that would be a little more reasonable.
I do not intend to name the various groups who should receive assistance under this bill. The veterans of the South African war have already been mentioned several times. I would put in a word, however, for the non-pensioned widows, some of whom are finding it very difficult to get along today. They are not as young as they used to be; they have done a good job, and they deserve some assistance. Then there are the imperials and others who have been supported so strongly by many hon. members, more especially by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks).
In conclusion, let me say that these old soldiers and the widows of old soldiers either deserve adequate treatment, or do not deserve anything. Surely they deserve that adequate treatment, because the minister has said so. But I do not think we should be so niggardly. What we should do is to give them what would be a defence against poverty in their old age, and we ought not to be content just to give them partial aid. After all, when they

reach the age some of these men have reached $40 a month is not very much, particularly when they cannot earn anything for themselves. It is poverty.
I hope that when the bill returns from committee it will be an entirely different looking product from what it is now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are going to find that a great number of veterans will be disappointed in the bill unless, while in committee, it is revised so as to give those in distress much more consideration than the bill in its present form affords. I am not a member of the committee, and for that reason I should like to speak briefly this evening.
Let me say at the outset that I concur heartily with the appeal made so eloquently by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), who spoke more effectively than I could ever hope to do. I agree with everything he said. This evening I have in mind one particular case, and I should like to bring to the attention of the house one point which I believe has not been discussed by any other member. I do not wish to repeat figures which have already been given. However I would refer to a soldier who came back from the war several years ago. This man was discharged in 1934 as having a heart condition. Dependent upon him were a wife and four children. He was discharged from the army with a ten per cent pension, was unable to do anything and indeed was confined to his bed. Because of his heart condition he was told not to,exert himself in any way. After appealing for a reboard, he went back to the hospital for observation.
This man was let out a second time, again with a ten per cent pension. That was in March, 1944, and I did not know anything about the ease until the fall of that year. During that length of time his wife had found it necessary to use all their spare money saved from the purchase of war bonds, and they had reached the point where they were fit subjects for relief. This man, however, was too proud to ask for relief, and his pride even prevented him from coming to see me to ask if I could do anything for him.
Let me say at once that I am glad to give credit to the department because, when I intervened on this man's behalf, his pension was increased immediately, I am told, to 100 per cent. They gave him $50 and also an allowance for each of his children, all of whom were under sixteen years of age. This brought in a total sum of about $90.
After a year he was reboarded and given observation, with the result that his pension

War Veterans Allowance Act
was cut, although he was still unable to do any work, and was under doctor's care. This man was told not to exert himself in any way but, periodically, he would feel better and would attempt to do some gardening or other light work. Each of those times he would have to go to bed for two or three days. His pension was cut from S50 back to $30, or thereabouts. It has been cut further since that time, and the second to last occasion he appeared for a reboard it was cut again.
This man is still unable to do anything. The oldest child has in the meantime reached the age of sixteen years, so that the father does not receive any allowance for him. That boy is out trying to earn a livelihood for himself. The family is, however, in next to destitute circumstances. I was in the house this winter and one could not tell by the temperature of the room if there was any heat in the building or not. I know this man could not afford to buy fuel. I do not know how much fuel he had in the house, or whether he had any. But I do know one could not feel any heat in that building. Surely that is a disgraceful condition.
The point I am making is this, that when this man went to hospital for a reboard he was not allowed to say anything on his own behalf. If he attempted to tell them anything he was told either to keep quiet, or that they would send him out. That is not right, surely. A man with a heart condition does not always look as sick as some others not suffering from that ailment might look. But I do not know how a man's condition could be ascertained unless the man himself were asked to give the symptoms, and to tell something about himself. Surely it is not right to have a man in hospital for observation, and then not permit him to speak on his own behalf. That is not fair and should not be allowed.
I hope that when the bill goes to committee the minister will reconsider it, and that if the recommendations in the bill are not sufficient he will redraft it so that these men will get what is rightfully theirs without having to have others intervene on their behalf. Why should we as members of parliament have to intervene for men who have served their country faithfully and well and then, upon discharge, find that they have disabilities for which they are not responsible? It is time parliament was big enough to look after these men without our having to make representations on their behalf.
Mr. ANGUS MaeINNIS (Vancouver East): Mr. Speaker, at this late hour in the debate, after so many members have spoken in favour of a more generous measure than the one now before us, there is very little one can say
that has not already been said. However, since I am not a member of the veterans affairs committee, and since I have received many letters from veterans, not only recently but over a number of years, complaining of the inadequacy of the allowance, I wish to add my protest to those which have already been made. Also I would add my hopes, if they are worth anything, to those who have already expressed the hope that the minister will reconsider the measure either before or after it goes to the veterans affairs committee, and bring something forward more worthy of Canada than this bill.
I examined the bill for a considerable time before I could find where there was any amendment to the act. This is a bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946. I have in my hand a leaflet issued by the war veterans allowance board, giving information in regard to the 1946 act. I have also examined the 1946 act and I have found it difficult to discover what the amendments are. Undoubtedly there are some amendments. I did find one amendment, early in the bill. That is an amendment increasing the salaries of the members of the board from $6,500 to $7,000.
After that very good start by those who drafted the measure, I was hoping they would carry it on for those who are supposed to benefit from war veterans allowances, those for whom the War Veterans Allowance Act was enacted, and not just for those who were administering the act. Persons who are required to administer an act of this kind ought to be well paid because they have to do a dirty job. The act provides $365 a year for a single person.

A dollar a day.
Mr. MaeINNIS: A dollar a day, and in a leap year it will be just one dollar less than a dollar a day. This is a leap year and I imagine these men will have to go hungry for the extra day. Is there a member of this house who believes that he could live decently on $365 a year?

Mr. MaeINNIS: I appreciate what my hon. friend means, but we expect people to live
War Veterans Allowance Act

decently. I do not know how many single veterans are receiving this allowance, but they are supposed to live on $365 a year. The minister shakes his head, but I will read the relevant section. There could not have been much in the heads of those who drew up this act, whether they were shaking them or not. Section 4 reads:
The maximum allowance payable in any year to an unmarried veteran or a veteran bereft by death of his or her spouse, without child or children, shall be three hundred and sixty-five dollars less the amount of any income of the recipient in excess of two hundred and fifty dollars per annum.
If he has not $250, if he has not anything beyond the $365 he will have only the $365 on which to live. The basis of the allowance should, in my opinion, be a living allowance in itself. If this great, rich country cannot provide a living allowance for the men who risked their lives for their country, then there is something very wrong with the members of this house and with the government of this country. What amazes me is the difficulty of improving the standard of living of persons with low incomes. If one has an income of $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 it is not difficult to add another $1,000 every two or three years, but if a person is receiving less than $1,000 or less than $500 he must live on that because there is no hope in the world that he will get anything more.
I have jotted down some of the reasons why we should be more generous with war veterans than we are in this bill. The first thing that struck me is that we could afford to be. This is a rich country and at the present time the government is fairly flush with funds, if I may use that term. For that reason alone we should be more generous. If a man treated an animal the way we treat these people he would be brought up in the courts for cruelty to animals.
The second reason is that we are seeking recruits for the armed services. When a young lad finds his father or his grandfather subjected to this sort of treatment after having risked his life for his country, what hope is there that the young man will be eager to join some branch of the services? There is not the slightest hope in the world. The third reason is that there is a great ado at the present time about the danger of communism. Communism is not something that just happened for no reason whatsoever. Communism developed under the autocracy of czarist Russia. It did not develop in countries where freedom and justice existed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it is a disease. Perhaps it is and perhaps it is contagious. When people are subjected to the conditions under which it developed in the first place they are more liable to catch the disease than those who are not subjected to the same -conditions, the same as with any other disease. If there is one thing that creates divisions and sets people against each other it is inequality, the feeling on the part of some that they are being discriminated against, that they are not receiving their fair share after they have performed their fair share of the duties required of a citizen. I suggest to the minister and to the government that they pay heed to the pleas that have been made in the house this afternoon, and that when this bill comes back from the committee it will be a better bill than the one we have before us. There will not have to be a great many changes made to make it a better bill, but I hope the changes will be made.
There is another point I wish to make. I cannot imagine why the single person for whom the government makes the magnificent allowance of $365 a year should not be allowed to earn at least that much more by his own efforts. Why is it that he is not allowed to have additional income of more than $250? If he earned more than that who would be hurt? Who would be hurt if he earned $500? I suggest to the minister that the more the individual recipient of war veterans allowance is allowed to earn, the better it will be for the individual and the better for Canada. Nothing can be worse for the individual than the continual frustration of not being allowed to earn a living income by his own efforts, to be denied that right without being penalized for earning more than $250.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) wanted to know the basis of these allowances.
I wonder if someone would explain how it was that somebody-that somebody who convinced the minister and the cabinet-came to the conclusion that $365 is sufficient income for a man who had offered his life for his country and who is not now able to make a living for himself by his own efforts? Would somebody explain just how the conclusion that $365 was a sufficient income was arrived at?
