subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to parliament in 1940 I have taken no part in the discussion of veterans problems because they have been handled very well by the veteran members of our group and other veteran members of the house. Since 1945 the veterans of world war II have joined the veterans of world war I, and I feel, in justice to the people of my constituency who are affected by this legislation, I could not let it pass without expressing my protest.
In the first place I do not wish my remarks to be considered by the minister as personal at all. I ami sure that every member of the house and the citizens of Canada are proud of his record in world war I and world war II. I know something personally, too, of the high esteem in which he was held in the University of New Brunswick before coming here. I am sorry for the minister that it is his misfortune to pilot legislation of this type through the Canadian parliament in the year 1948.
In the February issue of The Legionary, an article appears by the general secretary of the Canadian Legion which uses very moderate language:
Our idea of a new rate for war veterans allowance would be $50 per month for the single person and $85 per month for a married couple.
In an editorial in the same issue The Legionary says, speaking of the government's proposals for increasing disability pensions and war veterans allowances:
To many pensioners and to all war veterans allowance recipients the tremendous increase in actual living costs is nothing less than catastrophic.
These aging men and women are not concerned with the jump in automobile prices, or the higher cost of nylon stockings or cosmetics. They were already leading a marginal existence before the price increases and were not able to afford luxuries then. What they are vitally and desperately concerned about now is the price of bread and milk and butter and meat, and of shoes and everyday clothes and other things that are needed to exist. About the only bright spot in the whole gloomy picture is the fact that rents have been allowed to remain stationary, or nearly so.
These men, who offered their lives in the hour of Canada's greatest need, have earned a better deal than that which the government is proposing to give them.
The minister's officials have come to the conclusion that the cost of living warranted something being done. As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has mentioned, provision is made in the bill for board members, who receive a monthly cheque of $541.66, to get an increase of $41.67 because of the increase in the cost of living. They are to have extra take-home pay of $41.67 a month. It is very difficult for me to understand why a man getting $541.66 a month must have his salary increased to $583.33 because of the increase in the cost of living, while at the same time it 'is expected that single veterans getting $30.41 can get along with an extra $10 a month, or $40.41, and married veterans get along with $70.83, an increase of $10 over their present $60.83.
A little over a year ago I happened: to be present at a public meeting in the city of Montreal when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was making one of his first public statements as minister of that department. He spoke of the contribution that Canada had made during the war and said that dt had been our objective to see that no man who put on a uniform for his country would be any worse off for doing so and that no one who remained at home would be in any better position for having done so. He mentioned that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who also represents a Montreal seat, was doing his part to see that those who remained at home would not be in any better position than if they had gone to war. He also mentioned the present minister's predecessor, who also was seeing to dt that those who fought for Canada would not be in a worse financial position for having joined the force.
I think members in all parts of the house are agreed that veterans who have to get along on the provision we have had in effect of a maximum of $640 for a single person and $1,130 for a married person certainly does not put the veteran in a preferred position. I know a great many veterans who thirty years ago could not establish the fact that sleeping in the mud or being forced to go without sleep hour after hour impaired their physical health, but many of them are now in the evening of life. According to the minister's own figures, 16,711 veterans of world war I will be entitled to the full $10 a month, which means that they are to get by on $640 for a single person and $1,130 for a married person. That is the maximum, and many will get less.
War Veterans Allowance Act

If there were any question of Canada's not being able to afford to pay more the veterans would accept their lot without a great deal of complaint, but we are all proud of the magnificent performance of Canada during the war and there is no indication in the world, either in the field of construction, in the sale of automobiles, in travel or anything else, that Canada is now on the verge of bankruptcy. I looked up Hansard of February 11, 1944, to find out how we were prepared to spend money in those days. I find that the Department of National Defence was able to get 128,000,000 for capital expenditure on construction, purchase, repairs, and operating expenses of properties; $51,000,000 for repairs, operating expenses and rentals; $182,000,000 for ammunition and bombs; $104,000,000 for armament, including rifles, machine guns, mortars and guns of all descriptions; $274,000,000 for motor transport vehicles, trucks, tractors and trailers; $30,000,000 for the operating cost of mechanical transport. Now the minister comes to parliament and asks for only $14,000000 odd for the twelve-month period to discharge our responsibility to veterans of world war I, and world war II. Mr. Speaker, that is just not good enough. I feel sure that if the minister and the members of the committee cannot bring back to parliament proposals making more generous provision for the veterans who risked their lives for Canada, a great number of Canadian people will lose faith in the ability of Canada to keep her commitments to those who risked their lives for her in time of trouble.
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate with interest and noted carefully the criticisms and suggestions made. As I have listened this evening it has occurred to me, as it probably has to other members, that this 9th day of April, 1948, marks thirty-one years exactly since the first Canadian corps, which contained many of the men about whom we have been speaking during the last day or two, stonned Vimy Ridge and made a great name for itself. I am sure the survivors of that old corps will be glad to know of the generous feeling on the part of this house as reflected by the speeches that we have heard from all comers of the chamber both yesterday and today. Sandwiched in between the expressions of individual generosity there has been some criticism, but it has been a source of gratification to myself to note that those in the department, the board, who administer the work have not come in for any serious criticism in their administration of the act, whatever criticism may have been directed against the act itself. The work of those

administering the act has received due recognition. But that is only a small segment of the whole veterans program of Canada.
It has been stated by some that these amendments are not very important, while others have said that they are downright niggardly. All I wish to say in reply to such statements is that ever since 1930 in this house, and quite properly, the War Veterans Allowance Act has been held up as one of the finest pieces of veterans legislation in this or any other country for the purpose for which it was designed. I believe that is true, and I am sui-e hon. members believe it is true. If it is, then these amendments are very valuable for they improve that act for the veterans by approximately one-third.
The amendments are important because they increase the amount to the recipient. They are important, too, because the adjustments of the permissible income ceiling, and the other features related to it, give effect to those increases to the maximum degree.
There has been discussion of eligibility under this act, not touched upon by the amendments. I am not going into that tonight. There could be a long discussion as to where the cut-off line should be. There was at one time a school of thought from the old war that suggested that only those beyond the old artillery horse lines ought to be eligible for these benefits, because they were the only people who were really in a position to be preaged or to have serious after effects on account of active war experience and hardship.
That school of thought, I am glad to say, has not prevailed and for the old war the English channel was taken as the cut-off line. Arguments might be advanced if the Atlantic ocean were made a cut-off line; as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) so admirably pointed out, there might be some discussion as between zeppelin bombing and Salisbury Plain, on the one hand, and the experiences, which the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) might relate, in the explosion that occurred in Halifax, which killed sailors and soldiers, and which were attributable to the war. There might also be added some of the hard, cold camps such as Valcartier in those days.
I expect that in future years there will be discussions as to whether the Atlantic is the proper cut-off line for the new veteran, but that can await future discussions.
The question has been raised: what is the basis of this war veterans allowance? Hon. members know as well as I do, perhaps better, the basis of the original allowances set up in the original act. Whatever that was, I will

War Veterans Allowance Act
not attempt to define it tonight. In setting up the increase in these amendments, I certainly feel, however, that it should not be done without some consideration being given to the whole Canadian population; in other words, to the relationship between this increase and social security legislation such as old age pensions.
In reply to a number of hon. members, the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe), the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and others, I may say that these amendments will make the benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act greater than the combined federal and provincial benefits of old age pensions in any province in Canada.

speechtext:
I should like to go into that more fully in the committee, and I will let my statement stand until refuted at that time. I will, however, add this. The attempt has been made in working out these amendments to do precisely what I have said.
The statement has been made that the increases are subject to the approval of the board. Of course they have to be subject to the approval of the board, but that has carried with it the matter of the means test, and I am free to say that I am not very much more keen on that term "means test" than any other member of this house. Somehow it implies taking a person into a cold room and putting him through a close examination in respect of all factors entering into his life and living.
I can tell the house that in the administration of this act the members of the board and their staff look upon this part of their work under the act as an endeavour to help the veteran, a study of the difficulties which he has to meet through no fault of his own, and that attitude toward the work will continue.
There is one point I should like to emphasize. It has been suggested that the present recipients of the war veterans allowance must in all cases undergo a further investigation of their financial condition before this proposed increase can be paid to them. As somebody said, they must make application and by some method let it be known that they would like to get this increase and that they are qualified to get it.
That is not the case. The government has given special consideration to this matter. It was desired that this bill be so prepared as to enable the full increase to be paid immediately to all cases where existing records show the maximum allowance is now being paid and the 5849-181J
recipient is not now in receipt of income up to the new permissible income created in this bill; and we now know who those veterans are.
The practical effect of this will be that the main body-not quite all; I will refer to that later-of present recipients, based upon the recent study of records at the head office of the board which has now been carried out, will be paid the full $10 increase retroactive to October 1, 1947, immediately after this bill is ratified by parliament and the remaining group will be dealt with equitably by the board with the utmost dispatch and understanding immediately thereafter.
That bears upon the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo. He referred to page 2788 of Hansard and the statement I made yesterday afternoon in which I referred to a third group. I did not attempt to divide them into groups, except to try to give some definition of the veterans who have been under study by the members of the board during the past few weeks. Groups 1 and 2, as already referred to, can be dealt with right away or automatically, if you like, now that the study of the file has been completed. In the third group referred to there will be some-I cannot say the exact number tonight -following that study, who will be able to receive the full increase. There will remain perhaps one-third of the whole number of recipients from whom some further information may have to be obtained.
Hon. members will know full well that each one of those 26,000 or 30,000 cases, as they are called here, are human beings made of flesh and blood, with individual and complex sets of circumstances that are happening today, tomorrow and the next day. I spoke of the attempts of the department, in conjunction with the placement service of the Department of Labour, to get these men placed in work, encouraged to work, assisted in finding their way back, if they possibly can, with this veterans assistance grant as a backlog underneath to help them. We will take a man now receiving the grant who, we believe-according to the last discussions we have had with him, and the assistance that has been given him-hopes to get into a permanent or semipermanent job. If I were to say that on this date or whatever date this bill becomes ratified, he will get the increase, it would mean one of those things which no veteran likes, namely, the necessity of a government department asking for a refund in the future. So there is an attempt there in what I referred to yesterday as the third group, to tidy these things up ahead of time in order to make as few as possible subject to investigation when the bill is ratified.
Human Rights

During the debate there has been some discussion to the effect that some worthy veterans are reluctant to apply for war veterans allowance because they consider it a dole and feel that there is a stigma attached to it. I can assure the war veterans allowance recipients that nothing is farther from the minds of those who administer the act; I know that nothing is farther from the minds of the members of this house; and I believe that nothing is farther from the minds of the people of Canada. I want to make this quite clear. The War Veterans Allowance Act is, in my opinion, social legislation designed to help to meet the needs of some of the older veterans who have rendered valuable service to their country and who have been unable to gain full employment. I should like to repeat that the war veterans allowance is not in any sense a dole or a charitable payment. The spirit in which the act has been administered so far is the spirit in which these increased benefits -contained in the amendments will be administered by the members of the board.
When this bill receives second reading, I shall have much pleasure in moving that it be referred to the committee on veterans affairs.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the committee on veterans affairs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice, for the Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That it is expedient to appoint a joint committee of both houses of parliament to consider the question of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the manner in which those obligations accepted by all members of the united nations may best be implemented;
And, in particular, in the light of the provisions contained in the charter of the united nations, and the establishment by the economic and social council thereof of a commission on human rights, what is the legal and constitutional situation in Canada with respect to such

rights, and what steps, if any, it would be advisable to take or to recommend for the purpose of preserving in Canada respect for the observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms;
And that Messrs. Beaudoin, Breithaupt, Cour-noyer, Croll, Deehene, Diefenbaker, Fournier (Maisonneuve-Rosemont), Fulton, Hackett, Han-sell, Harkness, Hazen, Herridge, Ilsley, LaCroix, Maedonnell (Muskoka-Ontario), Marier, Marquis, Michaud, Massey, Miller. Probe, Rinfret, Robinson (Simcoe East), iSmith (York North). Stewart (Winnipeg North), Stuart (Charlotte), Whitman, Zaplitny be members of such committee, as far as the interests of this house are concerned.
That the committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records and to report to the house from time to time.
That a message be sent to the .Senate requesting that house to unite with this house for the above purpose, and select, if the .Senate deems advisable, some of its members to act on the said proposed joint committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether it will be possible, in view of the lateness of the hour, for the house to give this measure sufficient consideration tonight to enable it to be passed. I would hope so. In any event, I shall content myself with a somewhat brief statement of the facts relative .to the resolution. Apart from the names of the proposed members of the committee, the resolution is the same in terms as a resolution passed by the house last session. Pursuant to that resolution a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was set up. That committee met on June 5, June 13, June 17, June 20, June 26, June 27, July 4 and July 11, a total of eight meetings. It made four reports to the Senate and the House of Commons. Those to the House of Commons were dated June 6, June 17, July 12 and July 14. The general public made no oral representation to the committee, though a number of letters and I think, petitions were received which are now in the committee records. However, the deputy minister of justice was heard in regard to the legal and constitutional position of Canada in so far as human rights are concerned. The chief of the first political division of the Department of External Affairs gave evidence concerning the obligations assumed by Canada as a member of the united nations; and the director of the division of human rights, department of social affairs, united nations, appeared and supplied information relative to the activities of the united nations in the matter of human rights.
I should like to direct the attention of hon. members to the terms of the resolution. It will not be necessary for me to read it again since you, Mr. Speaker, read it a few moments

Human Rights
ago; but the interpretation placed upon the resolution by the committee last year was that it naturally falls into two divisions, the first dealing with the obligations Canada assumed as a signatory of the charter of the united nations, and the second relating to the steps it may be desirable for this parliament to take, irrespective of its obligations as a signatory of the charter of the united nations, in respect of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
With regard to the first division of the resolution to which I have referred, I think I should bring the house up to date with respect to what has happened since the committee ceased its deliberations last year and made its report. The commission on human rights which functions under the economic and social council of the united nations had a somewhat important meeting in Geneva from December 2 to December 17 of last year. This was the second session of the commission on human rights; and it has submitted a report of its proceedings and conclusions. This report has now been submitted to member governments of the united nations by the secretary general, with the request that the observations, suggestions and proposals of the various member governments with respect to the draft bill reach the secretary general by the 3rd day of April, 1948.

That was received in January; and this resolution was placed upon the order paper with the hope that there might be an opportunity for the house to consider the resolution and for the committee to give the government some advice as to the suggestions that might be made to the united nations before April 3. That was not found possible, so the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) wrote a letter to the secretary general of the united nations which I shall now read, with the consent of the right hon. gentleman. This letter is dated Ottawa, April 1, 1948, and reads:
Sir,
I have the honour to refer to your letter of January 9, 1948, in which was enclosed a report on the second session of the commission on human rights, and to inform you that the proposals contained in the draft international bill of human rights have been closely considered by officials of the government, and it is expected that they will be considered by a joint parliamentary committee on human rights. A discussion of this subject by parliament has not yet been possible, however, and the Canadian government would not wish to express views on a matter of such importance without having had
the benefit of learning the opinion of parliament. This is especially true in view of the nature of the Canadian constitution, and the Canadian government, therefore, regrets that final comments on the declaration will not be available for April 3.
The Canadian government is anxious that ample opportunity be afforded to comment on the international bill of rights both at the meeting of the economic and social council in July and at the meeting of the general assembly in September.
It is the opinion of the Canadian government that the final drafting of an international bill of rights is a serious task involving the reconciliation of differing philosophies and judicial principles. It is therefore respectfully suggested that the final expression by the united nations of human rights and fundamental freedoms may well require much more time than is at present contemplated, and that postponement of approval of the draft bill from the 1948 to the 1949 session of the general assembly might be with advantage taken into consideration.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
Louis S. St. Laurent, Secretary of State for External Affairs.
As I say, that letter was addressed to the secretary general of the united nations, Lake Success, New York.
I should like to say a few words with regard to the report of the commission on human rights, but perhaps I can shorten what I intended to say by referring hon. members to the Canadian Bar Review of March, 1948, where at page 548 they will find a short statement by Mr. John P. Humphrey, director of the division of human rights, united nations, setting out the present position, and a short description of the report. This report contains an account of the work of the commission, together with a draft international bill of human rights, presented in three annexes. It has been agreed that the term "International Bill of Rights" shall be understood to include (a) a draft international declaration on human rights; (b) a draft international covenant on human rights; and (c) the measures of implementation. It was on all three sections of the international bill of rights presented in the report as annexes A, B and C, that the comments of the member states were requested.
The draft declaration, when its final form has been settled, will be submitted by the economic and social council to the general assembly of the united nations for adoption, by a resolution of the general assembly as a statement of the human rights and the fundamental freedoms contemplated by the charter.
The authority for the resolution will be article 10 of the charter under which the general assembly may make recommendations to
Human Rights

the members of the united nations or to the security council, or to both, on any questions or matters within the scope of the charter. The declarations so adopted would therefore have the character of a recommendation and would not have absolute juridical force. That this is the accepted understanding of the juridical effect of the declaration is apparent from the report of the working group on implementation.
The declaration, while not a lawmaking document, would no doubt have a highly persuasive character; it could be appealed to as a political rather than as a legal argument by individuals considering that, in relation to themselves, there had been a violation of its provisions. It might also, in the course of time, be incorporated in whole or in part into the common law as a reflection of public policy. But whether or not the declaration would have this sort of effect upon the common law is speculative.
I have been talking about the declaration. As contrasted with the declaration, the covenant which is found in annex A is proposed as an international convention which will, upon ratification, become binding upon the states party thereto. The covenant in its present, or in other similar forms, will create binding international obligations which states will have to discharge by legislation, in so far as there is any inconsistency between the terms of the covenant and the state of its domestic law.
This being the case, it is apparent that the covenant should be scrutinized with the greatest possible care. The conclusion of international agreements is a prerogative matter which rests as a matter of law exclusively with the executive. There is, thus, no positive requirement of parliamentary approval or sanction before the ratification of a covenant such as the one now under consideration. However, it is well established constitutional practice that important international agreements imposing obligations on Canada or purporting to affect rights and interests within Canada are submitted, before ratification, for the approval of the houses of parliament by way of resolution.
The joint parliamentary committee, when set up, will of course be master of its own procedure. If the same scheme or organization is adopted this year as was set up last year, there will be a steering committee. But it would seem appropriate for the joint parliamentary committee in its division of its responsibilities to consider, first, annex A of the international bill of human rights; that is, the declaration. This part of the draft bill defines 
the principles upon which the international covenant, annex B, is expected to be based. It is suggested that these principles should be considered prior to an examination of the proposed international covenant.
It is suggested further

and more properly as I say, these suggestions should be made to the committee rather than to the House of Commons; but the House of Commons will want to know why they are setting up this committee, and something about what the committee is expected to do-that the committee might find it appropriate to examine only annex A, namely, the declaration, to begin with, rather than all three annexes of the proposed international bill of rights. At the next session of the general assembly it is possible that only the declaration will be considered for approval, while the covenant, annex B, may be referred for further consideration to the international law commission. In this event, the Canadian delegation to the next session of the general assembly would have to express approval or disapproval of a resolution embodying only the general principles outlined in the declaration, annex A. The covenant, annex B, would not be submitted in final form to the member states for some considerable time. For this reason, although comments on all three annexes were requested by the secretary general, it may be found advisable by the joint parliamentary committee to give its consideration first to the declaration only.
That will be, I assume, one and probably the first branch of the committee's duties. I may say that the question as to what steps nations should take with reference to this international bill of rights was considered in the British House of Commons. The debate is to be found in British Hansard, the issue of February 26, 1948, particularly at pages 2268 to 2276. This question as to whether nations should favour entering into a covenant creating international obligations, or whether they should be content with a declaration setting out principles alone, and having very much less binding effect, was given some consideration.
The Minister of State, Mr. McNeil, said this, bearing somewhat on the point about which I have been speaking:
It is quite plain, as every hon. member -who has spoken tonight has said, that it is not enough that we should have signatures to a treaty. There have been treaties in the past to which the signatories were nothing more than signatories. We must, in these most troublous times, also ensure that this treaty is enforceable and enforced.

Human Rights
And later he said:
We want definition, we want as wide and free an agreement as possible, and we want to be quite firm in ensuring that this is not just another pious resolution. I agree with the point about the peoples of eastern, and unfortunately, central Europe. We can, by disseminating the reports from the commission, by publication and by broadcasting the speeches, keep alive the idea; but let us be quite sure that we are unanimous that this is an enforceable covenant. That will be, I am sure, the wish of all sides of this house.
On that question I assume the committee would wish to make some recommendations. But, as I say, the declaration is the first matter to consider, rather than the covenant, which is much more definite and a much more difficult matter.

speechtext:
As a matter of fact there is not much more in Professor Humphrey's summary than I have 'told the house. There is much more in this declaration and in this covenant, but they are too long to put on Hansard. However they will have to be communicated to members of the house in some way so that they may have an opportunity to see what they are.
If I may I shall come to what was regarded last year as the second division or another division of the duties of this committee, although I must say that the duties of which I am now going to speak are closely allied with the duties I have been discussing. The committee was asked to consider and make recommendations as to what steps, if any, we should take an this country, apart altogether from our obligations as signatories to the united nations.
In that connection the committee decided last year that the attorneys general of the
*provinces and the deans of the law schools should be communicated with and invited to submit their views as to whether the dominion parliament has the power to enact a comprehensive bill of nights applicable to all of Canada, and that such written views be forwarded to the Minister of Justice. I think it would be appropriate at this moment if I were to state the results of that inquiry.
There is no record of a reply from Alberta. A reply was received from British Columbia stating that the attorney general of British Columbia is of opinion that most of the matters relating to human rights discussed by the committee appear to fall within provincial legislative jurisdiction and are for the most part dealt with and safeguarded by the common law, which is part of the law of British Columbia.
An acknowledgment only was received from Manitoba, and the same is true of New Brunswick. A reply was received from Nova Scotia saying that in the view of the attorney general, because of the distribution of subject matters of legislation between the dominion and the provinces as contained in the British North America Act, and because a bill of rights would affect both subject matters that belong to the dominion and subject matters that belong to the provinces, the parliament of Canada would not be competent to enact a comprehensive bill of rights applicable to all of Canada.
There was an acknowledgment only from Ontario. There was a reply from" Prince Edward Island stating that the attorney general considers that it is doubtful whether such a statute could be drafted so as not to conflict with the provisions of the British North America Act. There is no record of a reply from Quebec.
A reply was received from Saskatchewan. The attorney general of Saskatchewan considers that it would be presumptuous for him as attorney general to attempt to advise the committee on matters of law. He forwards a copy of the Saskatchewan bill of rights passed in 1947. In his opinion, the dominion can go much farther than the province did in the realm of criminal law in giving protection against arbitrary arrest or detention and in guaranteeing the right of habeas corpus and the right to assistance of counsel. He states that Saskatchewan is in favour of a federal bill of rights.

Before I pass on to deal with the replies of the deans of the law schools, I think I can sum up the result of this correspondence in this way. No attorney general says affirmatively that he is of opinion that the dominion parliament has power to pass a comprehensive bill of rights applicable to all of Canada; certain attorneys general express a negative opinion and deny that power, and several show very little or no interest in the matter. The general course and tone of the correspondence, when taken with that of the deans of the law schools, make it fairly clear that if the dominion government does undertake to set limits to the activities of the provinces in dealing with civil rights of this kind, it is altogether probable that a considerable provincial rights controversy will be precipitated.
This is perhaps borne out by the replies from certain deans of law schools. A reply was received from Dalhousie University as well as from Laval University. There is no record of a reply from McGill University, Osgoode Hall law school, the University of Alberta and the University of British Columbia. An acknowledgment was received from the University of Manitoba. There is no record of a reply from the University of Montreal, the University of New Brunswick and the University of Saskatchewan. A reply was received from the University of Toronto.
I shall not undertake to summarize the opinions of these deans because they are contained in an exhibit before the committee, but generally speaking they are most unfavourable to an affirmative answer to the question as to whether this parliament has that power. It will be the duty of the committee to consider these replies and decide whether they want to press for further replies, whether they should hear representations from the general public and from the number of organizations which have requested to be heard, as to what is legally possible and what is desirable in regard to this matter.
That is the present status of this matter. Briefly it can be said that we set up this committee last year but were not able to get very far on account of the pressure of work. We gave an undertaking to reappoint the committee this year, and the work which the committee can usefully do has been outlined in the few remarks I have made tonight.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I say that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) has properly outlined the events that have taken place since the committee met. While he was generous enough to say he felt that this resolution could well

be passed this evening, I am not as optimistic as he was. There is one thing that I have noticed. From the time that this matter was first mooted in this house, namely, the drafting of a bill of rights for Canada, and later on a request on the part of the united nations for assistance from Canada in the drafting of an international bill of rights, little support was received from the government of this country. That, sir, is very well supported by the fact that in January last the draft of the united nations organization, which believes that an international bill of rights is necessary if peace is to be preserved, was thought of so little importance by the government of this country that the matter has remained there secret until this evening, in spite of the fact that reference was made to that question on February 13, when I asked whether the government had received the draft and whether it would be submitted to the committee. Yet all the time the government knew that the nations of the world, meeting as they have been to draft an international bill of rights, were expecting an answer by the 3rd of April. That indicates, more clearly than words, how disinterested the government of this country is either in a national or in an international bill of rights.
I have very little time this evening before the adjournment of the house, but I am going to face one situation which the minister reiterated tonight, as he so frequently did in the committee, namely, the danger, because of the constitutional position of our country, of Canada passing a bill of rights.
Here we are a sovereign nation among the nations of the world and promising as a signatory of the united nations to uphold fundamental freedoms as one of the principal prerequisites for the success of the united nations; yet the minister's attitude tonight raises a doubt whether Canada even internationally can do that which all the nations of the united nations undertook to do when the charter was accepted.
We were circumvented last year in the committee by the constitutional issue being raised on every possible occasion; and the minister tonight reiterated the summation of the answers given by the attorneys general of the provinces and by the deans of the law schools, apparently believing that those answers, coupled with the evidence given before the committee, would once and for all end in this country the crusade for a national bill of rights and would determine as well Canada's position as being unable to discharge her international responsibilities.
The committee, if it is to meet as it did last year, will merely be shadow-boxing, going

Human Rights
through motions, postponing and procrastinating, with the government forever hiding behind the constitutional position.
The Supreme Court Act makes provision for determining this question once and for all. Time is going to deny me the opportunity to read section 55 of the Supreme Court Act, but I am going to sum it up in this way. When important questions of law or fact arise, touching the interpretation of the British North America Act, the constitutionality or interpretation of any dominion or provincial legislation, or concerning the powers of the parliament of Canada or of the legislatures of the provinces or of the respective governments thereof, whether or not the particular power in question has been or is proposed to be exercised they may be referred by the governor in council to the supreme court for hearing and consideration.
Then it says that the determination on that question of reference, although advisory only, shall, for the purposes of appeal by His Majesty in council, be treated as a final judgment of the said court between the parties.
Let us get away from this sham battle. Let us ascertain once and for all whether or not we have the power to discharge, first, our responsibility as a nation in the united nations, and, second, if a bill of rights is necessary for Canada, of which I suggest recent abrogations of civil rights in Canada indicate the necessity. Let us determine the question once and for all. For that reason I intend to move, seconded by Mr. Casselman, the following amendment to the resolution:
That the following words be added at the end of paragraph 2 of the resolution:
"that in order to assist the committee in its deliberations the government do immediately
submit to the Supreme Court of Canada such questions as are necessary to determine to what extent the preservation of the fundamental freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly and the maintenance of constitutional safeguards of the individual are matters of federal jurisdiction.
That, Mr. Speaker, once and for all will determine this question, so that no longer will anyone be able to hide behind the concept that under our confederation Canada cannot maintain the fundamental freedoms of Canadians within Canada. I now move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
